properties.evidence: This idea's own counter said it first: "the stall is about conquest having no PERMANENCE, not about willingness to attack... motion rather than progress." The 2026-08-28 history review reached the same conclusion independently and it became the accepted ruling. The earlier idea saw it coming.

That earlier idea recorded the AI ignoring supply convoys entirely — a system that WAS designed in. It saw this coming: an opponent that skips a shipped mechanic will certainly skip one the player invented afterwards.
The AI never sends a convoy, so the wagon's effect on a real game is unmeasured rather than measured — the harness returned byte-identical numbers because the thing it measures does not use supply.
Roads make supply cheaper along them; an AI that never supplies anything would not notice a road network existed.
River and sea supply would be equally invisible to the AI and to the harness until the AI uses convoys at all.
One sixty-turn run is an anecdote. Narrowing why the AI cannot finish a passive player needs many games played to a conclusion, which is exactly what the harness would do.
Four asymmetric houses means four games to balance instead of one. Without win rates per house, an asymmetric game is just a game with one correct choice.
Diminishing returns changes what every county produces from the same workforce, and nothing currently says whether the result plays better — only that it still runs.
Fixing permanence removed the revolving door and left this underneath: with the interior solid, the war is decided at a frontier neither side can push through.

Taking that idea's advice produced this: draftHarshness was the first shared constant turned into a per-ruler weight, and the measurement immediately showed the weight cutting the wrong way for the ruler it characterises. Wiring doctrine to real levers forces exactly this kind of question.
The baseline measured zero decided games in twenty and traced the oscillation; this node is the set of things that could be done about it.
The playtest is what raised this question: it set out to judge whether trade felt worth doing and found the answer was no, for reasons underneath the marketplace rather than in it.

properties.note: The current tile build is deliberately seed-free and deterministic — same output every run. Rasterisation must preserve that.
Circuits are laid out from the map's own order and a wagon advances by an index step, so no seed is consulted and routes are reproducible.
Named explicitly because this is the capability the prohibition is worded around — the moment a turn is resolved is exactly when a remote or generative call would be most tempting and most damaging.

The core is where the prohibition actually binds: it resolves turns, and it is the thing that must stay dependency-free and replayable from a seed. Any model-assisted authoring must hand it finished data, never a call.

properties.evidence: The siege resolves engines against a single defenceMultiplier. A castle made of choices needs a siege that can tell one part of it from another, so the spatial version of this idea replaces the current model rather than extending it.
The just price makes starving a county for profit shameful and costly. Burning one for advantage is worse, and if raiding carries no standing cost the design says the greater cruelty is the free one.

That requirement carries the manual's model, in which standing armies are paid wages and desert when the treasury falls short. Feudal terms of service are a deliberate step away from the source toward history.

The marketplace now prices grain at seven crowns in a starving county and one in a glutted one, and rewards carrying food into a famine. The just price says that act is the sin, not the strategy. Both cannot hold unqualified — the design has to decide whether the market is amoral or watched.

That requirement says systems mirror the manual's documented relationships before new features are layered on. Playing the game against the manual shows the biggest divergences are not new features at all but manual systems never built — the merchant marketplace above all — and a starting position (three counties) that contradicts the manual's explicit single county.

Option (d) would end these games by recognising a dominant realm rather than requiring every rival dead, which reopens an accepted decision. Recorded so choosing it is a deliberate reversal rather than a drift.

The manual describes no technology of any kind, and that requirement says the manual's relationships come first. A tech spine is the least faithful idea in this set and the one most clearly outside the source material.

That requirement carries the manual's county model, which includes one treasury shared across the whole realm — stone bought anywhere is instantly available everywhere. Catan-style scarcity requires the opposite. Both cannot hold, and the design will have to pick.

One says armies should be forced out of the field in winter; the other says the interesting move is refusing to leave. Both can hold only if wintering in the field is possible AND expensive, which has to be designed rather than discovered.

The shipped hex map does not meet this and cannot as built: it derives land from a radius around hand-placed county centres, so the silhouette is a union of circles. Recorded as opposing rather than satisfied, because drawing a SATISFIES edge here would claim the requirement is already met by the very thing that fails it.

properties.evidence: The personality traits that would carry the asymmetry already exist and already drive the AI. Extending them to modify the human player's economy and combat reuses that table rather than adding a system.
Pricing and AI-awareness of authored objects are only questions once authored objects exist; this is the consequence half of that idea.
The movement allowance is recomputed every turn from the army's slowest unit, so a seasonal modifier has an obvious place to live.
A ruler could not order a castle at all until the build control was added on 2026-08-26; designing one is that control grown up.
The coastline work gave counties real terrain — mountains, hills, moor, coast, rivers — and castles currently ignore all of it. Siting is nearly free because the ground is already there.
A grammar that generates one number is pointless — there must be features to generate before generation means anything.
Foraging is already "an army strips the county it stands on". Raiding is that machinery with intent, plunder and consequences added.

Debasement and coin scarcity both act by moving prices, so neither means anything until there is a market where prices are paid. That market now exists and already carries a supply multiplier these would ride on.

That idea already proposes turning aggression from a gate into a real weight over how far an army will march and how outnumbered it will fight. This is the same work reached from the other direction, so it lands on top of that one rather than beside it.
Foraging is already "an army does something to the county it occupies" — it eats the stores and starves the land. Raiding is the same machinery with intent, so the hard part is built.
Pillaging is listed there as one of the manual's own systems that was never built. Axis & Allies is pointing at a hole the source material already named rather than importing something foreign.
One ruler's doctrine only means something inside a scheme where rulers carry doctrines; the Knight as Machiavelli is the first instance of that idea, not a separate feature.
Every claim here is sourced from that transcribed manual, re-read in full on 2026-08-26 rather than skimmed as it was during the adopt pass.

Within-county detail — visible fields, a county town that grows, roads — has nowhere to live until counties are made of enough tiles to hold it. The presentation question is only answerable after the resolution question.

Which option is right here turns on how many maps get authored. One Britain map makes the cheap rasterised-coastline route sensible; five maps amortise a file format and an editor and make the fully-authored route sensible. The map-shape question cannot be answered well before the how-many-lands question.
The whole point is that the machinery already exists — opinion, gifts, insults, alliances, decay and the opinion bands are built and tested. This idea only supplies new actors to aim it at.

A player-authored object has to be switchable off per game — the sandbox-only option in dec:idea-authored-object-balance depends on it outright, and no scored game should silently inherit another player's invention. The design already has a per-game optional-rules switch, so this idea rides on it rather than needing its own.

Measured, not assumed: aggression is read twice in the whole AI and both times as a threshold, and ten games at aggression 1 matched ten at aggression 3 on identical seeds. A doctrine layer over traits that do nothing would be four philosophies with one behaviour, so making the traits real levers has to land first.
Choosing which rulers to model is only worth anything once it is settled which decisions a ruler's beliefs actually reach; otherwise the doctrines are a table nothing reads.
Catan-style trade is worthless until a marketplace exists, and the missing marketplace is the second finding in that gap list. This idea is a shape for that hole, not an alternative to filling it.
Seasons elapsed and the besieged county's remaining stores are both already tracked by the siege system; the attrition keys off numbers that exist.
Fog of war already models a realm seeing only what it has been near, so there is somewhere for a scouted-or-not distinction to live.
Specific counters need specific things to counter; against a single defence multiplier there is only ever one way in.
This is the how-is-it-built half of that idea; if the player never authors objects there is no populate step to model on anything.

The template is a Python service calling OpenRouter over the network, so it can only be transferred at all under the authoring-time-only answer to that question; the offline deterministic core cannot host it in any form.
A network of strongpoints means nothing until a ruler can actually order castles built, which only became reachable in the UI on 2026-08-26.
Britain-only was settled, so regional bonuses have just three countries to work with and two of them are lopsided. Whether sub-regions must be authored is decided by that one-map choice.
The convoy already walks a route tile by tile and can be intercepted; the change is a per-tile deduction inside a step that exists. Without convoys there is nothing for a wagon to eat.
The rivers on hex edges and the Coast terrain already exist and are currently used only as an obstacle and a colour; this reads the map that is already there.
Cheap water carriage only means something once land carriage has a cost. Without the wagon eating its load there is nothing for a river to be cheaper THAN.
Where the model runs is only a question if the player is authoring objects with one; this is the execution half of that idea, not a separate feature.
Choosing which slots to open is only worth anything if the authoring mechanism lands at all; if that question is answered no, this one evaporates.

The river-works slot — the user's own blocks-in-a-river example — is only meaningful once rivers carry supply and movement semantics that a built thing can interdict. That is exactly what water-is-the-artery proposes, so the most interesting slot here is downstream of it.

The existing hex map, terrain and rivers capability is the older form of this thought: it already gives each county a cluster of hexes with terrain and edge-rivers. This idea is that capability grown up — the same model with an authored coastline instead of a derived one.

This requirement is the road taken out of that brainstorm: Ajs promoted the map-shape idea to intent on 2026-08-26. The decision stays open because it holds the unanswered HOW — raise resolution, rasterise a real coastline, fully author tile files, or the hybrid — while this requirement records the WHAT, which is now settled.

"A Britain scenario playable end to end" is the older, narrower form of this question. Asking which lands exist is that requirement grown up into a question about how many maps the game carries and what balance each is built for.

The balance harness showed this capability never actually reaching a decision in 20 games. This ruling is the chosen direction for making it do so: conquest that compounds, plus capitulation as an ending short of grinding a realm to zero.

properties.evidence: That idea was recorded as RISKS against both req:deterministic-sim and req:offline-mobile-play. This constraint is the answer to that hazard: it closes the option that caused it (a model inside the turn loop) while leaving the two viable options open, so the idea can be explored without the requirements being quietly at risk.

It gives a ruler a way to hurt a rival that does not require taking fortified ground — which is precisely the thing the measured stalemate says cannot be done. A front unbreakable by assault might still be broken by hunger behind it.

Option (a), pricing against local supply, delivers most of what the Catan scarcity idea wanted — goods worth different amounts in different places — without breaking the shared treasury the manual describes, which was that idea's blocking objection.

That question asked how to give the economy a ceiling, and supply pricing supplied an economic one. This supplies the moral one the playtest left missing, using the happiness and reputation systems that already exist.

Option (d) of that question was demand-led production. Diminishing returns is the supply-side half of the same fix: a mine whose marginal worker produces almost nothing stops flooding the realm with stone nobody wants.
The harness measured a leader ending with 180,000 units of materials nothing consumes. Castles saturate at one per county; a road network is a continuous sink for timber and stone.
A supply radius with no roads is a wall a player discovers; with roads it is a problem they can solve by investing. Rome's answer to logistics was infrastructure, not better carts.

Variety without uncertainty is a bigger lookup table, not a better game. Imperfect information plus the seasons an engine already takes to build is what turns a castle's design into a wager rather than a calculation.
That question asked how castles relate to one another. This one asks what a castle IS — and a network of fortresses that are each a single number is a network of one repeated fact.

That requirement says a county's surplus must become money and scarcity must show as a price. A store with no ceiling defeats it: four of eleven goods are pinned at the price floor precisely because surplus accumulates without limit, so the price signal saturates and stops meaning anything. A capacity or spoilage rule is what would keep the signal alive.

Partially, and only the first half. Closed vocabulary axes declared in code answer the 'player writes their own numbers' hazard by making the code own the vocabulary and the model only choose within it. It does nothing for the second half — the AI still will not know an authored object exists — and the descriptive/generative split means storyflow's own validation story does not come with it.

Conquest currently has no structural brake — measured in a headless run, one AI ruler reached 21 counties by year 6 with nothing pushing back. Overextension strain is a hazard-answer to exactly that runaway.

The stall is a UNIFORM grind where every part of the front is equally impossible. A supply radius does not make offensives easier, it makes them possible in some places and not others — turning a featureless meat grinder into geography, which is the shape a war game wants.

The measured stall is that an army deep in enemy land cannot be reinforced, so every push falls back to where it started. A fortified camp is the period's own answer to exactly that — not going home is what turned Viking raiding into conquest in 865.

The playtest found nothing worth buying after year one. Wool is the first good the realm would make to SELL rather than eat, and a cloth trade gives the market's buy side something a realm actually cannot produce for itself.

The SVG map and HUD views replaced the Phaser canvas as the game's renderer. The canvas was already outside the game loop and opt-in behind ?phaser=1; on 2026-08-28 the user ruled it retired rather than documented.

That question asked why the AI could not finish off a PASSIVE HUMAN, and guessed at causes. The harness showed the AI cannot finish off ANOTHER AI either, and named the mechanism, so the narrower question is answered and superseded.

The measurement behind this idea — ten games at aggression 1 against ten at aggression 3, same seeds, identical medians — is evidence that one of this capability's advertised dials is very nearly inert. That is a hazard to the claim that AI behaviour is adjustable, whether the answer is to make the dial real or to relabel it.

The constants are acknowledged as educated placeholders with a tuning pass owed, and there is no balance harness. Four asymmetric houses means four games to balance instead of one, so this multiplies an already-unpaid debt.

The balance baseline checks a fixed set of designer-priced elements. An object whose numbers the player chose at play time is outside anything that baseline can have measured, so authored objects would let a game drift past the check without the check noticing.
Advanced Farming already models seasonal weather and is an option a player can switch off. Two seasonal systems behind different switches would leave it unclear which one is making the winter hard.
Victory is by total conquest and total conquest is unreachable: a realm that cannot be consolidated out of existence cannot be eliminated, so the only win condition the game has never fires.

The harness deliberately plays every realm with the SAME AI so that anything moving between runs came from the design rather than from play. Per-ruler doctrines break that premise: telling Edward I from Robert the Bruce needs rulers assigned per seat and win rates by doctrine, which is a harness mode that does not exist.

Wages and desertion are currently the only brake on armies growing without limit. Levies that cost no wages remove that brake, so the term of service has to replace it — and if it does not, the game gets easier rather than richer.

If a ruler's documented temperament reliably makes him weaker once it is made mechanical, then grounding rulers in history produces a table where the best-characterised opponents are the worst players. That is a hazard to the whole idea and worth settling before a table of doctrines is built.

The Prince is 1513 Florentine and the game is 1268 Britain, so this puts a deliberate anachronism inside a design whose whole appeal is period grounding. Recorded as a risk rather than a fault because the anachronism can be made the characterisation — the Knight playing by rules the mirror-for-princes tradition calls dishonourable — but only if it is chosen on purpose.

Both halves change how much a county produces from the same workforce, which moves food, population, happiness and revolt together. Nothing currently measures whether the result is better, only that it still runs.

Two map scales roughly doubles the client's UI surface, and the accepted quality target for this project is maintainability — things that change together living together. This idea pulls directly against that target, which is the strongest argument for answering it "one scale".

Ferry links exist because specific county neighbours are separated by water that land pathfinding cannot cross, and they are enumerated against the current derived coastline. Replace the coastline and the ferry list is wrong until it is re-derived or re-authored — Cornwall, Argyll and Caithness are exactly the places a real coastline changes most.

Movement is a per-turn budget spent on a pathfound route where terrain sets the cost. Changing tile resolution changes every distance in the game at once, so the movement speeds and the siege and convoy pacing tuned against the current map would all need retuning.

Victory is decided by "last realm standing". Modelling neutral counties as realms would mean the game could never end, so this idea threatens the outcome logic unless minor lords are deliberately kept outside the realm count.
Total conquest remains the only way to win, and a front that grinds indefinitely means it is still never reached — measured to 125 game years.

Progression is not a system beside the others; it is a modifier on production, combat, castles, farming and conscription at once. The accepted quality target says things that change together should live together, and a tech tree changes together with everything.
It makes taking fortified ground harder, and fortified ground is already nearly untakeable — on its own this could deepen the measured stalemate rather than break it.

Determinism was justified in the READMEs by the hosted-split and lockstep goal. Dropping multiplayer removes that justification while leaving determinism just as load-bearing for save/load resume and for the 168-case suite — so the requirement risks being discarded along with the goal that happened to argue for it.

Untested but plausible: the baseline currently shows a leader hoarding six figures of materials while fielding 250 men, and a realm that cannot hoard must spend. Recorded as a risk to the baseline's current reading rather than as a claimed fix, because the connection is assumed and not measured.
A control radius makes the map stickier at exactly the point the harness says it is already too sticky to break, so it wants to arrive after something that makes offensives possible, not before.
Ferries already move armies over declared sea links. A second water system that does not know about the first would be two answers to the same question.

An LLM is not deterministic, so consulting one inside the turn loop would break determinism from a seed. Freezing the model's output to data before the sim ever reads it is what keeps this requirement true.

A model call is a network call, and this requirement says the Android build plays fully offline. Only the authoring-time-only option leaves the requirement intact; the other two either fight the APK budget or break it outright.
Natural Earth is public domain: no attribution, no share-alike, and geography is fact rather than anyone's artwork. Chosen over OpenStreetMap's ODbL coastline for exactly this reason.
This is the capability the accepted rasterised-coastline decision calls for. Marked planned, not full: nothing is built yet.
The constants were always in one cited place; what was missing was any way to tell whether changing one helped. This supplies the measurement half.
The column is fed from its own cargo per tile travelled and struck from the map once it has eaten itself hollow.
Gives the market a good produced expressly to sell, which the playtest found it lacked.

properties.description: Sheep graze the pasture that counties already hold, sheared each season into the realm's shared stores by shepherds drawn from the labour pool, capped by how much pasture the land carries. properties.name: Wool
Army fan radius now derived from banner geometry rather than a flat guess, fixing the stacked-army bug at three or more armies.
properties.subject: system

properties.name: Restoring the correct baseline. britain.ts is UNCHANGED by the coastline work — the previous accept mistakenly stamped britain-tiles.ts's hash onto this artifact, which would have hidden a future edit to britain.ts.
properties.subject: system

properties.name: Map shape: authored coastline replaces derived land
properties.rationale: The island's silhouette was a union of circles around ~90 hand-placed county centres, which is why the map read as bubbles rather than as Britain. Inverting the dependency — geography decides the coast, counties fill it — is the smallest change that fixes it. The lesson worth keeping: the complaint was about the coastline, not about counties being single hexes, and the cheap fix aimed at the wrong one.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: The Britain tile map stops deriving land from a radius around county centres and instead rasterises a real coastline as a land mask, assigning land hexes to their nearest county. Tile resolution rises at the same time, because a coastline cannot be expressed at roughly five hexes per county. Not yet implemented — recorded to see what it touches before any code is written.

properties.name: A captured county is garrisoned from the army that took it
properties.rationale: The balance harness measured the reason no game ever reached a decision: a county walked into and left empty is one the enemy walks back into next season. At turn 200 only three of eighty owned counties carried a garrison, and territory oscillated for forty years without anyone being consolidated out of existence. Garrisoning from the taking army is what a medieval captain actually did, and mechanically it makes holding land cost army strength — so a thin raiding force must now choose between taking counties and keeping them.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Capturing a county now detaches a holding force from the capturing army — half a castle's full garrison where there are walls, a token watch on the town where there are not — taken from the cheapest troops in the ranks so a captain leaves levies at the gate and keeps his knights for the field. The army never falls below the minimum legal size doing it, so an army too small to spare anyone takes the county but cannot hold it.

properties.name: Movement constants retuned for the coastline map
properties.rationale: The factor was measured, not guessed: the median journey between adjacent county towns went from 3 movement points on the old map to 7 on the coastline map. Scaling by that restores the old feel almost exactly — the share of adjacent counties an army can reach in one turn is pikeman 65%-63%, foot 79%-82%, knight 90%-97%. Knights come out slightly more mobile than before, which suits their role as raiders. Relative speeds were kept in proportion so combined-arms composition still decides pace.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Unit speeds, the army and convoy movement budgets, the river-crossing penalty and the exploration vision radius all scaled by the measured 2.3x change in map distance. Pikeman 3-7, peasant/crossbow/sword 4-9, maceman/archer 5-12, knight 6-14; army fallback 5-12, convoy 4-9, river crossing 2-5, vision radius 2-5.

properties.name: Three defects found by playing, fixed
properties.rationale: All three were found by scripting a play session rather than by any test, and none of them threw an error — which is why they survived a suite that was already green. The stacked-army one is the likeliest cause of the report that the game "didn't seem to work": mustering a second army silently made the first unselectable, with nothing on screen to say two were there. The lesson worth keeping is that a passing suite said nothing about whether the game could be played; the checks now cover the interaction, not just the state.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: Armies sharing a tile now fan out onto a small ring instead of stacking exactly, so each keeps its own clickable area. The owner palette names all five realms a game can hold, and every lookup falls back to a visible colour rather than none. The turn log reports the player's own realm plus map-wide conquest and diplomacy, instead of every event in all 82 counties. Three Playwright regression tests added, each confirmed to fail when its fix is reverted.

properties.name: The legacy art shell capability is retired with its canvas
properties.subject: system

properties.name: The legacy Phaser canvas is retired
properties.subject: system

properties.name: Prices answer local supply; merchants have a purse
properties.rationale: The playtest found the marketplace mechanically sound and economically pointless: nothing worth buying after year one, and one county's grain worth 58 times the realm's whole tax income. Fixed prices made the market a vending machine. Two things were needed and neither alone was enough — pricing against supply makes hoarding visibly worthless and turns trade into a question of where and when, while the purse is what actually caps the exploit, because even at a floor price a granary of 25,000 sacks is a fortune. The purse and the price scale together on both sides of every trade, which is what keeps buy above sell at every supply level and so leaves no arbitrage loop.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary: A good's price is now a fact about a good IN A PLACE. Each good has a reference holding — a year's food for grain, a per-county allowance for materials and weapons — and the price moves against the ratio of what is actually held to that, bounded between a fifth and triple the base. Merchants also carry a finite purse and a finite cartload, refilled when the wagon moves on, so no granary can be emptied into gold in one visit.

properties.name: Nothing generative or networked may be consulted inside the turn loop
properties.statement:
The simulation core must never consult a non-deterministic or networked source while resolving a turn. Anything produced by a language model — or by any other generative or remote source — must be frozen into validated, plain, inspectable game data BEFORE the core reads it, and the core must treat that data exactly as it treats hand-authored content.

This is a prohibition, not a budget. It holds on every platform, not only Android, and it holds whether or not any model-assisted authoring feature is ever built. Distinct from con:offline-no-network, which says the Android BUILD must work with no network: this says the simulation CORE must not depend on one under any circumstances, and adds the freeze-to-data rule that constraint does not carry.

It exists to protect two things the design already holds — req:deterministic-sim (the same seed must give the same game) and req:offline-mobile-play — against a class of future change rather than against one feature. A model consulted mid-turn breaks replay, breaks save compatibility, breaks offline play, and breaks the test suite's ability to assert anything, all at once and quietly.

properties.decision:
Two changes to the conquest rules, chosen 2026-08-28 to answer the balance harness ending 0 of 20 games decided:

1. A pacified county contributes back — levy capacity and income — so taking ground stops being a permanent decrement to the conquering force. Today GARRISON_ON_CAPTURE = 0.5 pays every conquest out of the field army with nothing flowing back, so offensive power decays with each victory.

2. A realm reduced below a threshold capitulates, surrendering its remaining counties, rather than having to be ground to zero county by county.

Scoped as a direction, not an implementation: the thresholds, the pacification period before a county contributes, and what capitulation hands to whom are all still open.
properties.name: Conquest must pay for itself, and a beaten realm capitulates
properties.rationale:
Grounded in the history the user asked for. Conquerors who FINISHED had conquest financing the next conquest — Rome's socii and citizenship turning conquered manpower into Roman manpower, the Ottoman timar granting conquered land out in exchange for the cavalry that took the next land, the Mongols incorporating defeated troops and funding campaigns from tribute. Conquerors who STALLED paid to hold ground out of the field army with no return: the Crusader states permanently short of men because every castle held was men not in the field, Napoleon with ~200,000 troops tied down holding Spain. constants.ts:358 records that GARRISON_ON_CAPTURE was itself the fix for an earlier revolving-door stall — it solved that and encoded the Crusader-state failure in its place, as its own comment concedes: "A thin raiding force can take counties or hold them, not both."

Capitulation is the second half because history says conquests ended politically — realms surrendered, defected or were partitioned. Total conquest county-by-county is the rarest outcome there is, and 34 sieges won against 0 eliminations is exactly what a ruleset with no capitulation produces.

properties.decision: All tunable numbers live in a single constants module, each with a citation to the manual passage behind it.
properties.name: Keep every balance number in one table, each cited to the manual
properties.rationale: The manual is qualitative and fixes no numbers, so the constants are acknowledged as educated placeholders — keeping them together and cited makes a tuning pass possible instead of a treasure hunt.

properties.rationale: Stated as a convention: domain rejections are not transport errors, so a client can distinguish 'you asked wrongly' from 'the world says no'.
