properties.rationale: Two stated project goals drove it: remake the manual faithfully first, and split frontend from backend for an eventually-hosted online game. Because state is plain data and transitions are deterministic, the same core runs server-authoritative and is amenable to lockstep.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Found by the balance harness, 2026-08-27, when turning aggression from 1 to 3 barely moved anything.

WHAT THE SETTING LOOKS LIKE. The new-game panel offers an "AI aggression x" field, and it multiplies every ruler's inherited aggression before their turn is planned.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY DOES. `traits.aggression` is read in exactly two places in the whole AI, and both read it the same way: `if (traits.aggression < 0.3) return null`. It is not a degree of anything — it is a single threshold, and above it every ruler behaves identically. The personalities sit at Knight 0.9, Baron 0.7, Countess 0.6, Bishop 0.2, so the ONLY ruler the multiplier can change is the Bishop, and only by lifting him over 0.3 into being willing to campaign at all. Everyone else is already over the line at the default and is merely clamped back to 1 by a larger multiplier.

MEASURED. Ten games at aggression 1 against ten at aggression 3, same seeds: identical median hoard, identical median sieges, identical decision rate of zero. The ranges did move — the smallest hoard went from 11,163 to 53,169 — so it is not wholly inert, and those are the games where a Bishop happened to hold a seat. But a dial whose effect depends on whether one of four temperaments turned up is not the dial the panel advertises.

WHAT COULD BE DONE, none of it decided.
Make aggression a real weight rather than a gate: how far an army will march from home, how outnumbered it is willing to be, whether it prefers a rich target or a weak one. The military planner already scores targets, so there is somewhere for a weight to go.
Or be honest and relabel it, since a setting that does almost nothing is worse than no setting.

⚠️ COUNTER, and it is the more interesting one. Making the AI more aggressive was already suspected to be the wrong fix for the game not ending; the baseline suggests the stall is about conquest having no PERMANENCE, not about willingness to attack. A better-tuned aggression dial might make the raiding faster without making it decisive — motion rather than progress.
properties.name: OPEN — the AI aggression dial is a switch with one hinge, not a dial

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Found by the overnight facet sweep, 2026-08-26.

THE MEASUREMENT. Three nobles, AI aggression turned to its maximum of 3, and a player who never issued a single order — no armies raised, no counties managed, nothing. Sixty turns, fifteen game years. The player was still holding counties at the end and the game had not been decided. Whatever the AI does with its aggression dial, it is not enough to finish off somebody who is not even defending.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. Victory is by total conquest, so a game that cannot be lost is also a game that is hard to win — the same slowness that spares a passive player is what makes a campaign drag. It also means every difficulty setting currently sits somewhere between "easy" and "easy", because the hardest setting available does not threaten a player who is asleep.

CANDIDATE CAUSES, none yet confirmed and all cheap to test.
The AI may not be mustering enough: earlier headless runs showed The Bruce reaching twenty-one counties by year six, so it expands into empty land well, but taking a DEFENDED county needs a siege and sieges take seasons.
The player's starting castle is garrisoned, and a garrisoned castle can only fall to a siege — so a passive player is not undefended at all, they are behind walls the AI may simply never commit to breaking.
Movement was retuned for the new map and the AI's planning was not re-examined afterwards; distances doubled, and an AI that plans one march at a time will cover ground more slowly than before.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT. A headless AI-versus-AI harness that plays many games and reports how many reach a conclusion, in how many turns, and who wins. That harness does not exist, and its absence is why this is a question rather than a fix — the same missing measurement that the balance work keeps running into.

⚠️ COUNTER. Making the AI more lethal is easy and usually wrong: the failure mode is a game that kills a learning player in year two. The interesting fix is probably not "more aggression" but "actually commits to sieges", which is a planning change rather than a dial.
properties.name: OPEN — a player who does nothing survives sixty turns against three rivals at maximum aggression

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Found on 2026-08-27 by measuring the wagon change and getting a byte-identical answer.

WHAT HAPPENED. The convoy now eats its own cargo as it travels — verified in the simulation suite and measured on the map: six tiles keeps 81% of a load, forty-one keeps 23%, and the hundred and twelve tiles from Hampshire to Caithness keeps under 2%, so an ordinary cartload sent that far is struck from the map having eaten itself hollow. Then the balance harness ran the same twenty seeds and returned numbers IDENTICAL TO THE DIGIT: hoard 286,170, hungry county-seasons 5,662, sieges 16 laid and 34 won, revolts 21, plagues 492. Not close. The same.

THE ONLY EXPLANATION, and it checks out: the AI has never sent a supply convoy. Its whole command vocabulary is eighteen verbs and SendConvoy is not among them. Every AI army in every game has lived entirely off foraging the county it stands in.

WHY THIS MATTERS FAR BEYOND THE WAGON.
Logistics is currently a PLAYER-ONLY system. A human can supply an army in the field; no AI ruler ever does, or ever will, whatever is done to the rules. So every logistics idea in this brainstorm — the wagon, river supply, roads, winter camps — will be invisible to the harness and to the AI's war until this is fixed. The instrument cannot see them because the thing it measures does not use them.
It also reframes the stalemate. "Offensives cannot be sustained" was measured on an AI that has no means of sustaining an offensive and never tries. The AI is not failing to supply its armies; it does not know supply exists.
And it means the wagon change is currently unmeasured rather than measured-and-ineffective. It is correct, tested, and its effect on a real game is unknown.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT, none chosen.
(a) TEACH THE AI TO SUPPLY ITS ARMIES: a convoy when a field army's carried supply runs low and there is a friendly county in range to send from. This is the smallest change and it is the one that makes every other logistics idea measurable.
(b) Give the AI a notion of supply range at all, so it prefers targets it can reach and sustain — which is what a supply radius is FOR, and what would turn the uniform grind into geography.

⚠️ COUNTER. Teaching the AI logistics makes it better at war, and the game already cannot be finished; a smarter AI on both sides may simply grind more competently. Worth doing anyway, because until the AI uses the system nothing about it can be judged.
properties.name: OPEN — the AI never sends a supply convoy, so logistics does not touch its war at all

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list: StarCraft.

THE IDEA. StarCraft's three races are not reskins — Terran, Zerg and Protoss have different units, different economies and different win conditions, and choosing one chooses what kind of game you are about to play. The manual already hands this project four characters: the Bishop, the Baron, the Knight and the Countess. Today they differ only in AI temperament — the Knight is war-loving and refuses alliances, the others weigh diplomacy differently — but a human playing as any of them plays an identical game.

WHAT ASYMMETRY COULD MEAN HERE. The Knight musters cheaper and fields better cavalry but is poor at trade and diplomacy. The Bishop's counties are happier and recover faster, and he can call on the Church for gold, but conscription costs him double in morale. The Baron taxes harder without unrest and builds castles faster. The Countess trades and negotiates from strength, gets better prices and more reliable alliances, but fights at a disadvantage. Each of these is a modifier on constants that ALREADY EXIST, not a new system.

WHY IT IS A GOOD FIT. `NoblePersonality` and its trait table are already in the code and already drive the AI. Extending traits to modify the player's own economy and combat, rather than only the AI's choices, is the smallest version of this idea and it reuses the machinery wholesale.

⚠️ COUNTER, AND IT IS ABOUT BALANCE RATHER THAN CODE. The project's own README already admits the balance numbers are "educated placeholders" with a tuning pass owed, and there is no balance test beyond a single starting-food guard. Asymmetry multiplies that unpaid debt by the number of houses: four houses means four games to balance instead of one, and an asymmetric game that is not balanced is simply a game with one correct choice. Doing this well probably means owing a real balance harness first — headless AI-vs-AI runs measuring win rates per house — which does not exist.

SECOND COUNTER: it cuts against the manual, where the four nobles are characters and opponents rather than playable classes.

WHAT NOT TO TAKE FROM STARCRAFT. Real-time play collides with a turn-based county game — although note the original's BATTLES were real time, so a tactical real-time battle layer is the manual's own idea rather than StarCraft's, and is recorded separately. A supply cap would duplicate the wages system, which already limits army size by making it expensive.

COST. Small in code, large in balancing — the reverse of most items here, and the reason to be careful.
properties.name: OPEN — should the noble houses actually play differently? (StarCraft factions)

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Distinct from the mechanism and the slot questions: this one stands whatever answer those get, because it is about what happens after an authored object exists. Both halves would still need answering if the player authored objects through a plain form with no LLM anywhere near it.

TWO PROBLEMS, and the second is the harder one.

FIRST — the player is writing their own numbers, through a model that wants to be agreeable. "Blocks in a river that stop Viking longships" naturally reads as "stops raids". Ask for a stronger version and you get a stronger version. Whatever populates the object is being asked to price it, and nothing in the loop wants to say no. Options: hard-clamp every field to ranges the sim declares (cheap, and blunt — it caps invention at whatever the designer already imagined); price it against a cost curve so a stronger effect costs proportionally more (medium, and the honest version — it makes the authoring a trade rather than a wish); or let it be unbalanced on purpose and treat authored objects as a sandbox mode that never touches a scored game (cheapest of all, and it quietly admits the feature is a toy).

SECOND — the AI opponents will not use authored objects, will not counter them, and will not know they exist. The design already records this failure happening with a system that WAS designed in: dec:idea-ai-ignores-logistics says the AI never sends a supply convoy, so logistics does not touch its war at all. If the AI ignores a mechanic that shipped with the game, it will certainly ignore one invented after the fact. The player therefore gets a tool no opponent has and no opponent answers, which is a one-sided advantage no clamp fixes.

Options for the second problem: give the AI the same authored objects the player made (strange, but symmetric and cheap); express authored objects only through effects the AI's existing evaluation already reads, so it responds to the CONSEQUENCE without understanding the CAUSE (medium, and the most likely to actually work); or accept the asymmetry and only allow authoring in sandbox play (cheap, same admission as above).

THE OBSERVATION UNDERNEATH BOTH: the second option in each list is the same idea said twice — an authored object is safest when it is expressed in the vocabulary the sim and the AI already speak. That points back at the finding on dec:idea-player-authored-objects: the LLM can only fill shapes the sim already has holes for, and the shapes that keep the AI honest are exactly those holes.
properties.name: OPEN — a player-authored object is an "I win" button unless something stops it, and the AI will not know it exists
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-27 while thinking out loud. Recorded beside the idea rather than used to talk it down — but the AI-ignores-it half is grounded in a failure the design has already observed once, so it is not a hypothetical objection.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-26 after the same gap blocked four separate questions in one day.

THE PATTERN. Every balance question this project has raised ends the same way. Diminishing returns on labour: no way to tell whether it improves the game. Asymmetric noble houses: four houses to balance instead of one, with nothing to measure them. Giving the economy a ceiling: changing the food economy moves population, happiness, revolt and conscription together, and nothing says whether the result is better. And now the AI failing to finish a passive player, where the cause cannot be narrowed without playing many games. The README has said the balance numbers are "educated placeholders" with a tuning pass owed since before any of this.

WHAT IS MISSING. The suite proves the game still RUNS. Nothing measures whether it PLAYS. There is one balance test, guarding starting food, and that is the whole of it.

WHAT IT COULD BE, and it is smaller than it sounds because the core is already headless, deterministic and seed-driven. Run N games to a conclusion with no human, varying the seed, and report: how many reached a decision at all, in how many turns, which noble won, how far the realms diverged, whether anyone starved, whether prices sat at their floor or ceiling. Then a change is judged by what it did to those numbers rather than by whether the tests still pass.

WHY IT IS WORTH DOING FIRST. It is the difference between tuning and guessing, it costs one evening rather than a system, and every idea in this brainstorm currently carries the same caveat that this would remove. It also turns a whole class of finding from anecdote into evidence: "a passive player survives sixty turns" is one run and could be luck; "in ninety of a hundred games the human is never eliminated" is a fact.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It builds nothing a player will ever see, which is a real cost when the game still lacks things the manual describes.
A harness measures what it is told to measure, and picking the wrong measures would make it worse than nothing — a number that goes up while the game gets duller.
And determinism means a hundred seeds is a hundred samples of the same AI: it would say nothing about how a HUMAN experiences the game, which is the thing actually in question.
properties.name: OPEN — build the thing that can tell us whether a balance change helped

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-27 as part of making logistics real.

THE HISTORICAL FACT. Medieval armies did not campaign all year — they campaigned when there was grass for the horses and grain in the fields to forage, and they went home when there was not. Hosts mustered after the spring sowing and moved through summer and into autumn, living off a countryside that had something to give. Winter meant quarters, not marching: no forage, foul roads, and an army that stood still ate its own supply. The feudal term of service reinforced it — men owed a season, not a year. An army in the field in January was doing something exceptional and paying for it.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW. A turn IS a season, and the calendar already runs Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter with weather and seasonal grain labour under Advanced Farming. But an army marches exactly as far in January as in July, forages the same, and fights the same. The one system that most obviously wants seasonality has none.

THE IDEA. Tie campaigning to the calendar: movement shorter in winter, forage thinner, attrition on any army still in the field when the snow comes. The effect is that war acquires a RHYTHM — a campaigning season with a shape to it, a scramble to take ground before the weather closes, and a winter in which both sides recover and rebuild. That rhythm is most of what makes reading medieval military history feel different from reading modern.

WHY IT MIGHT MATTER FOR THE STALL. The harness found a front that grinds continuously for a hundred and twenty-five years. A season that forces armies to disengage and refit would break the grind into campaigns with beginnings and ends, and give an attacker a reason to concentrate for a push rather than trickle men forward forever.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It slows the game, and the game is already too slow to reach a decision — four turns a year with one of them dead is a real cost to pacing.
It also risks being pure friction: if winter simply means "nothing happens", that is three good turns and one wasted one, and players will click through it. Winter should DO something — recover, rebuild, negotiate, build castles — or it is dead air.
And it partly duplicates Advanced Farming's seasonal weather, which is an OPTION players can turn off; two seasonal systems with different switches would confuse.

COST. Small to medium. The calendar and the movement allowance both exist; this is a modifier keyed to the season, plus a decision about what winter is FOR.
properties.name: OPEN — armies march to the harvest: the campaign season

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-27: Lords of the Realm I had a castle designer he remembers fondly; Lords of the Realm II cut it to five or six fixed designs, and "I knew exactly how to defeat each castle type and how to protect them — so it became predictable and mechanical."

WHAT THE ORIGINAL ACTUALLY DID, from the Lords of the Realm I Castle Siege and Battle Manual. A castle was a FLOORPLAN, not a number. The siege screen showed walls and towers "in shades of gray, with the darker grays showing weaker areas (lower walls and smaller towers)". Walls were "much less sturdy than towers, gatehouses, and keeps". A gap in a wall let fighter units move INSIDE and attack the inner structures. Engines had ranges, so where you placed them mattered. Moats could be filled with earth by fighters with shovels, taking a season, during which they could be attacked. Five engine types, each with a use: ladders for low walls, towers for higher ones, catapults, trebuchets for heavy stone, rams for gates.

WHAT THIS GAME HAS NOW. `CASTLE_SPEC` gives each of five designs a wood cost, a stone cost, a work total, a garrison capacity, a tax bonus, and ONE `defenseMultiplier`. A castle is a scalar. There is nothing to design, nowhere to be strong or weak, and no reason to build one castle rather than the next one up the ladder except cost — which is exactly the predictability Ajs is describing.

THE IDEA. Make a castle a set of decisions with costs and consequences: wall height and thickness, how many towers and whether they are square or round, the strength of the gatehouse, a moat and whether it holds water, a keep, a well, a second ring of walls. Each choice buys resistance to a PARTICULAR kind of attack and buys nothing against the others.

⚠️ THE COST FORK, AND IT IS THE REAL DECISION HERE.
ABSTRACT — a castle is a bag of features, each a number, and the siege resolves arithmetically as it does today. Small, fits the existing auto-resolved siege, and could be built in a sitting.
SPATIAL — a castle is a small layout, and the siege is a targeting problem as in Lords I. Much larger: it needs a siege screen, placement, ranges, and a whole interaction model. It also cuts against a decision already taken, that battles are auto-resolved rather than played out — the core README records that deliberately.
These are not the same project. The abstract version gets most of the DESIGN interest for a fraction of the work; the spatial version is what Ajs actually remembers enjoying.

⚠️ SECOND COUNTER. Variety alone does not cure predictability — see the separate question about what a besieger is allowed to know. A castle with ten designable features and full visibility is a lookup table with more rows, and a player will solve it just as thoroughly, only more slowly.
properties.name: OPEN — a castle as a set of choices, not a menu of five

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs, 2026-08-27: "allow AI to develop some unique castles (probably can constrain in certain dimensions to avoid completely off the wall castle designs)".

FIRST HALF — SITING IS THE BIGGEST SINGLE FACTOR, and the map now supports it. What made a castle formidable was usually WHERE it stood before it was anything about how it was built. Edinburgh and Stirling on crags; Harlech on a rock above the sea it was resupplied from; Caerphilly and Kenilworth behind artificial lakes; Château Gaillard commanding the Seine. Rock foundations defeat mining outright. Water on several sides removes approaches. High ground breaks escalade and outranges engines. The coastline work gave this game real terrain — Mountains, Hills, Moor, Coast, rivers on hex edges — and none of it touches castles at all: a keep on a Cumbrian crag and one in the Cambridgeshire fens have identical defence. Letting the county's ground constrain what can be built and how strong it is would make WHERE you fortify a decision, and it costs almost nothing because the terrain is already there.

SECOND HALF — AI CASTLES FROM A GRAMMAR. Rather than picking from a list, a ruler's castle grows from a budget and a set of rules: what the ground allows, what the realm can afford in stone and timber and labour, and what that noble's temperament favours. The Bishop, whose trait table already gives him the highest build ambition at 0.8, raises walls; the Knight at 0.3 barely fortifies and spends on men. Constrain the grammar so every result is a castle somebody might actually have built — no gatehouse without a wall, no concentric ring before an outer one — and the variety comes out plausible rather than random.

WHY THE CONSTRAINT MATTERS MORE THAN THE GENERATION. An unconstrained generator produces novelty that is merely noise, and a player cannot learn anything from an opponent whose castles have no logic. A grammar with real rules produces castles that are DIFFERENT AND READABLE — you can look at one and infer what its builder feared, which is what makes an opponent feel like a person rather than a dice roll.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
Siting is cheap and safe; the grammar is neither. A generator needs a cost model good enough that it does not produce castles nobody could afford, or ones so cheap they are strictly better than the alternatives — and there is no balance evidence for any of these numbers yet, though the harness could now supply some.
Terrain-gated castles also risk making some counties simply better to hold, which is realistic and could quietly hand the game to whoever starts nearest a crag.
And both halves depend on the castle being a set of features at all — a grammar that generates one number is pointless, so this sits downstream of the castle-as-choices question.
properties.name: OPEN — the ground decides, and AI castles from a grammar rather than a menu

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-27, and it arrives with an odd piece of evidence behind it.

THE HISTORICAL FACT. In the Hundred Years War the English repeatedly found they could not reduce French fortresses at acceptable cost — so they stopped trying. The chevauchée was a deliberate strategy of mounted raiding that AVOIDED strong places and burned everything else: Edward III's march of 1346, the Black Prince through Languedoc in 1355 and again in 1356. The aim was not ground. It was to destroy the enemy king's revenue, wreck his ability to feed an army, and humiliate him in front of the men who owed him allegiance — a lord who cannot protect his people is a lord losing his people.

AND HERE IS THE EVIDENCE. The balance harness has just measured this game arriving at exactly the strategic situation that PRODUCED the chevauchée: a fortified frontier neither side can push through, sieges won a hundred and fifteen times across twenty-six counties, a war that grinds for a hundred and twenty-five years without resolution. The historical answer to that predicament was not a better siege engine. It was to stop attacking walls and start burning fields. The game has reproduced the problem and lacks the period's own answer to it.

THE IDEA. An army in enemy territory may raid rather than occupy: strip and burn a county's stores, wreck its fields, take plunder in gold, and move on without holding anything. It costs the victim revenue, food and happiness; it costs the raider nothing but time and reputation. Note the manual already has PILLAGING as its own section, and it was never built — so this is the source material's own mechanic as much as a history lesson.

WHY IT COULD BREAK THE STALL WITHOUT TOUCHING THE WALLS. It gives a ruler a way to hurt a rival that does not require taking a fortified county, which is the thing that cannot currently be done. A realm bled of food and gold cannot pay or feed its garrisons, and a front that cannot be broken by assault might be broken by hunger behind it. That is both good history and, potentially, the mechanism that lets a war end.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It cuts hard against the just price and the reputation system just built: burning a county is worse than profiteering in one, and if raiding carries no standing cost the design is saying that starving people for profit is shameful but starving them for advantage is free.
It could also become the dominant strategy and hollow the game out — why ever besiege anything if raiding is cheaper? It needs conquest to remain the only route to VICTORY, which the accepted decision already guarantees, so raiding weakens a rival without ever winning.
And it is the darkest thing in the design. The period's own texts are unromantic about what a chevauchée did to the people living there; a game can model it without dressing it up as clever.

COST. Medium. Foraging already strips a county's stores, so the machinery for "an army does something to the land it stands on" exists; what is new is the intent, the plunder, and the consequences.
properties.name: OPEN — the chevauchée: when you cannot take the castles, burn the country instead

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-26 on Ajs's instruction to keep the economics medieval — "not like they had central banks and fiat currencies and federal interest rates".

THE MEDIEVAL FACT. There is no monetary policy because there is no money in the modern sense — there is SILVER, struck into coin. A king cannot print; he can only mint what bullion he has. What he CAN do, and repeatedly did, is debase: strike the same number of pennies from less silver. Philip IV of France earned the name Philip the Counterfeiter for it; Henry VIII's Great Debasement is the notorious English case. It raises money fast, and it is found out — prices rise, good coin is hoarded and bad coin circulates, and the ruler's word is worth less than his coin.

The other half is BULLION FAMINE. Europe periodically simply ran out of silver — the fifteenth century badly — and when coin is scarce, trade contracts, prices fall and men return to barter and payment in kind whatever the harvest was like. Deflation with no bank behind it.

THE IDEA. Two dials, both physical and both with teeth.
DEBASEMENT as an emergency lever: raise gold now against a lasting penalty — prices rise (a straightforward multiplier on the existing supply factor), happiness falls, and rival nobles trust you less, which the diplomacy system can already carry. The classic desperate-ruler move, and the game currently has no way to raise money in a crisis except taxing harder.
COIN SCARCITY as a condition rather than a choice: when the realm's gold runs very low relative to the size of its economy, trade itself becomes harder — merchants offer less, and part of what you owe must be paid in kind. That makes the treasury a constraint on the economy rather than a scoreboard.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
Debasement is the more interesting and the more dangerous: it is an obvious trap, and a trap the player will only spring once. It earns its place only if the short-term relief is genuinely tempting, which means real tuning rather than a token penalty.
Coin scarcity risks a death spiral — poor realm, worse trade, poorer realm — which is realistic and miserable, and would want a floor.
Neither is in the manual. Both are firmly medieval.

COST. Debasement: small, one multiplier plus consequences on systems that already exist. Coin scarcity: medium, and it touches the market's pricing that has only just settled.
properties.name: OPEN — coin as a physical thing: debasement and bullion famine

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised by the balance harness's first finding, 2026-08-27: not one game in twenty reached a decision in fifty years, with every realm played by the AI. The measurement lives on ver:balance-baseline; this node is what to DO about it.

THE MECHANISM. The first ten years are a land grab — seventy neutral counties fall to twenty. Then the free land runs out, and for the remaining forty years the county counts oscillate: one realm reaches 46 of 82 and stops, the other two wobble between 12 and 25, and nobody dies. At the end, THREE of eighty owned counties carried a garrison and SEVEN armies stood on the map. Territory changes hands constantly because nothing defends it and nobody stays: an army takes a county, marches on, and it is retaken behind them.

SO THE PROBLEM IS NOT AGGRESSION, which is where the obvious fix would have gone. It is that taking a county does not KEEP it. Without permanence there is no consolidation, without consolidation no elimination, and elimination is the only way this game can end.

FOUR LEVERS, cheapest first, none chosen.

(a) A CAPTURED COUNTY GETS A GARRISON — an army leaves some of itself behind, or the county raises a token watch. Land then has to be taken from somebody rather than walked into, and a thin raiding force stops being able to flip half a realm.

(b) THE AI SHOULD FORTIFY WHAT IT HOLDS. It builds castles only when buildAmbition exceeds 0.6, which the Knight at 0.3 and the Countess at 0.5 never reach — the two most warlike temperaments never fortify anything they take.

(c) THE AI SHOULD MARCH AT CASTLES, NOT STUMBLE ONTO THEM. It lays a siege only against a garrisoned castle it ALREADY OCCUPIES, never setting out to take one. Three sieges in fifty years is the result, and the siege is the mechanism by which a defended realm falls.

(d) MORE ARMIES. Seven armies for eighty-two counties is barely a front line. The harness also found ZERO deserters in every game, so the wage brake never engaged — armies are not limited by cost, the AI simply is not raising them.

⚠️ COUNTERS. (a) is the strongest lever and the easiest to overdo: garrisons everywhere would make every advance a siege, slow in a different way. (b) and (c) are AI-side only, so a human who fortifies would just find the AI easier. And all four want re-measuring rather than reasoning about — which, for the first time, is now possible.
properties.name: OPEN — conquest has no permanence, and that is why the game never ends

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Distinct from the two ideas it serves: those ask whether to ground rulers in history and which ones. This asks what a ruler's beliefs would have to REACH before any of it shows up in a game. It would have to be answered whatever doctrines were chosen, and it is the question that decides whether the work is worth doing.

THE PROBLEM, measured and already in the graph. `traits.aggression` is read in two places in the whole AI, both as `if (traits.aggression < 0.3) return null`. It is a gate, not a degree. Ten games at aggression 1 against ten at aggression 3 on identical seeds produced identical median hoards, sieges and decision rates. So today a doctrine could say anything and change nothing.

CANDIDATE LEVERS, all of them decisions the AI already makes, so this is about reading a weight where a constant is hardcoded today rather than inventing new behaviour:
- WILL HE HIRE MERCENARIES? Already a decision (`HireMercenaries` when conscription lags and gold allows). Today it is one rule for everybody. Machiavelli says no; a 13th-century English king with Gascon crossbowmen says yes. One boolean, immediately visible.
- HOW HARD WILL HE TAX, and does he stop short of what the county would bear?
- WALLS OR PEOPLE? The castle-building versus happiness-spending choice. This is Edward I's iron ring against "the best fortress is not to be hated", and the game already has both spends.
- DOES HE PURSUE OR ACCEPT A SURRENDER? The capitulation rules built today make this a real fork for the first time.
- HOW FAR FROM HOME WILL HE MARCH, and how outnumbered will he accept a fight? dec:idea-aggression-is-a-switch already proposes exactly this as the fix for the dial, and the military planner already scores targets, so there is somewhere for a weight to go.
- WHOM WILL HE ALLY WITH, and will he keep faith? The diplomacy system exists; today personality only decides whether alliances happen at all.

WHY THIS ORDERING MATTERS. Every lever above is a place where the code currently holds ONE opinion for every ruler. Turning each into a per-ruler weight is small, additive and independently testable — and it is the same work dec:idea-aggression-is-a-switch already asks for, arriving from a different direction. The doctrines then become a table of numbers rather than four new planners.

⚠️ THE COUNTER: the balance harness cannot currently tell four AIs apart. It plays every realm with the same AI on purpose, so that anything that moves between runs came from the DESIGN rather than from play. Measuring whether Edward I beats Robert the Bruce needs a different harness mode — rulers assigned per seat, win rates by doctrine over many games — which does not exist and is real work in its own right. Without it, four doctrines would be four untested claims.

A SMALLER, HONEST FIRST STEP if this is ever taken up: pick ONE lever (the mercenary rule is the cheapest and most visible), give it to one ruler, and see whether a human playing against him notices. That is a cheaper test of the whole idea than building the table.
properties.name: OPEN — which decisions a doctrine would have to touch to be visible at all
properties.rationale:
Captured 2026-08-28. Recorded separately because it is the gating question for both other ideas and would survive either of them being dropped — and because the answer, a table of weights over decisions the AI already makes, is much cheaper than the four-planners reading the idea might otherwise invite.

TESTED 2026-08-28, and the answer is yes. The mercenary lever was built and measured over 8 games x 120 turns with personalities rotated across seats so no seat was favoured. Knight refusing hired swords against the same Knight allowed them:

  bands hired    0  vs  13
  avg counties   18.2  vs  28.3
  avg soldiers   130   vs  468

ONE BOOLEAN, wired to a decision the AI already makes, cost the Knight 36% of his territory and 72% of his army. So a doctrine grounded in a real text does produce a visibly different opponent, and the levers listed above are the right shape. That was the open question and it is now settled.

TWO THINGS THE TEST ALSO FOUND, neither of them expected:

1. THE KNIGHT WANTS MERCENARIES MOST. He hired 13 bands where the Baron hired 7 and the Countess 6, because he is the most aggressive and burns through men fastest. The doctrine bites hardest on exactly the ruler the text was chosen for, which is either perfect characterisation or an accident worth knowing about.

2. HALF A DOCTRINE IS A NERF, NOT A CHARACTER. Refusing hired swords is only half of what The Prince argues — the whole of it is "use your OWN arms". A `draftHarshness` trait was added to carry the other half (the Knight works his peasantry "to the point of cruelty", so he drafts hardest), replacing a hardcoded 0.5 every ruler shared. It recovered only part of the loss: 20.7 counties and 160 soldiers against the 28.3 and 468 of the control. The compensating lever is throttled by MAX_ARMY_TARGET and by what a county's population can bear, so mercenaries had been letting the Knight exceed what his own lands could raise. A doctrine needs its counterpart to be EFFECTIVE, not merely present.

WHICH CONFIRMS THE BALANCE COUNTER on dec:idea-asymmetric-houses empirically rather than by argument: one boolean turned the strongest AI into a middling one. Four doctrines would be four such effects interacting, with no harness able to tell them apart.

THE EXPERIMENT WAS REVERTED. The knowledge is the deliverable; shipping the refusal alone would be a balance regression rather than a feature.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised by the marketplace playtest of 2026-08-26, which found the market mechanically sound and economically pointless: nothing worth buying after year one, and one county's grain worth 58 times the realm's entire tax income.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS NOT THE MARKET. Production has no ceiling and food has no sink. Timber, stone and iron accrue at a flat 128, 36 and 15 a turn forever; the priciest castle costs 120 stone. Grain accumulates without limit or spoilage — Wiltshire reached 25,455 sacks in six years. The core README already names this: "carrying-capacity boom-bust", listed under known balance gaps, with a tuning pass owed.

FOUR WAYS OUT, cheapest first.

(a) PRICE AGAINST LOCAL SUPPLY. A merchant pays less for what a county already has heaps of and more for what it lacks. A granary holding 25,000 sacks fetches a pittance a sack; a county that has just been pillaged pays through the nose for bread. Cheap — it is one function between the stock level and the price — and it is the only option that fixes the exploit AND makes trade a decision rather than a vending machine, because now WHERE and WHEN you sell matters. It also delivers most of what the Catan scarcity idea wanted without touching the shared treasury.

(b) LET FOOD SPOIL. Grain above some multiple of what a county eats rots over the winter. Historically right, and it turns a granary from a bank into a buffer. ⚠️ The manual explicitly says only DAIRY spoils and that grain is storable and transportable, so this contradicts the source material — worth wanting anyway, worth knowing.

(c) GIVE MATERIALS A SINK. Castles are the only thing timber and stone are for, and one castle per county caps demand almost immediately. Roads, mills, walls, bridges, ships — anything that consumes materials continuously — would make the buy side live. Larger, and it is new content rather than tuning.

(d) MAKE PRODUCTION DEMAND-LED. A quarry that keeps cutting stone nobody wants is the actual bug; production could idle when stores are full, freeing that labour for something else. Medium, and it touches the labour system that the county game is built on.

NOT MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE: (a) and (d) address opposite ends of the same loop and would sit well together.

⚠️ COUNTER TO ALL OF IT: this is balance work on a game whose numbers the README already admits are "educated placeholders", and there is no balance harness beyond a single starting-food guard. Changing the food economy will move population, happiness, revolt and conscription all at once, and nothing currently measures whether the result is better — only whether it still runs. A way to measure would reasonably come first.
properties.name: OPEN — how do we give the economy a ceiling, now that the market has exposed it has none?

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list: Axis & Allies.

TWO THINGS AXIS & ALLIES DOES THAT THIS GAME DOES NOT.

FIRST, EVERY TERRITORY WEARS ITS VALUE ON ITS FACE. An A&A board prints an income number on each territory, so you can look at the map and see at a glance who is winning, which territory is worth fighting for, and what losing one would cost. Here every county looks alike and the only way to judge one is to click it — and the only way to judge the WAR is to count coloured hexes, which measures area rather than power. A ruler with three rich lowland shires may be stronger than one with ten Highland counties, and nothing on screen says so. This is the cheapest half of the idea: the number already exists in the simulation as tax revenue and production; it is simply never shown.

SECOND, YOU CAN ATTACK AN ECONOMY WITHOUT TAKING GROUND. A&A lets you bomb industry; you hurt the enemy's ability to make things without holding the territory. This game has exactly one verb for hostility toward land — take it — so war is all-or-nothing and there is no such thing as a raid. Notably the MANUAL HAS THIS ALREADY: pillaging is its own section, and it is one of the systems the manual describes that was never built. So this is not really importing an idea from Axis & Allies; it is Axis & Allies pointing at a hole the source material already told us about.

WHY IT FITS. Foraging and supply convoys are already a form of economic pressure — an army eats the county it stands in, and convoys can be intercepted. Raiding is the missing verb in the same family, and the machinery for "an army does something to a county it occupies" is built.

⚠️ COUNTER. Making counties visibly unequal will expose how unequal they already are, and that exposure is a balance problem the project has not paid for: the README calls the constants "educated placeholders", and county worth currently falls out of terrain and population without anyone having designed the spread. Showing the number invites the question of whether the number is any good. Also, a raid verb that is strictly better than conquest — damage with no occupation cost — would make conquest pointless, so it needs a real price: unhappiness, reprisals, a stained reputation with every noble watching.

COST. Showing county worth: small, and mostly a HUD change. Pillaging/raiding: medium, and it wants the reputation consequences to land with it or it unbalances the war.

WHAT NOT TO TAKE. Rigid turn phases (purchase, combat move, combat, non-combat move, place) would restructure a turn that currently works as one continuous season. Naval fleets are a weaker fit than they look: Britain is a single landmass and every county but Anglesey is joined by land, so a navy would be a large new system serving one crossing.
properties.name: OPEN — should counties have visible worth, and should you be able to hurt a rival's economy without taking his land? (Axis & Allies)

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-26 on Ajs's instruction to keep the economics medieval.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW. Every soldier draws a wage every season, and a realm that cannot pay watches its armies desert. That is a mercenary economy — early modern, and correct for the condottieri or a standing army, but not for 1268.

THE MEDIEVAL FACT. A knight held land IN RETURN FOR SERVICE. He owed his lord a fixed term in the field — customarily forty days a year in England — and he served it unpaid because the land was the payment. Past that term he went home, legally, however the campaign was going, unless the lord paid him to stay. That single rule shaped medieval warfare more than any other: it is why campaigns were short, why sieges were so often abandoned, and why kings who wanted long wars had to find another way.

The other way was SCUTAGE — shield money. A vassal who preferred not to march paid instead, and the lord used the cash to hire men who would stay as long as the money did. So a lord chooses each season between an army he cannot keep and an army he cannot afford, and that choice IS the medieval military economy.

THE IDEA. Split the host in two. Feudal levies cost no wages but serve a limited term each year and then melt away; mercenaries and paid retinues cost gold and stay. Scutage becomes a real income: let your vassals buy out of service and spend the proceeds on men who will finish a siege.

WHY IT FITS. It gives sieges the drama they historically had — the besieger racing his own army's departure date — and the game already has multi-season sieges, wages, desertion and mercenary bands. Most of the parts exist; what is missing is the term of service and the choice.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
This is a substantial change to a working system, and the wage-and-desertion model is currently what stops armies growing without limit. Remove the wage on levies and that brake goes with it, so the term of service has to do that work instead — and if it does not, the game gets easier rather than richer.
The manual has no feudal term: its armies are paid, and the remake is faithful there. This would be a deliberate step away from the source toward history.
It also adds a per-army clock the player must track, which is real cognitive load in a game that already asks a lot.

COST. Medium to large. It touches conscription, wages, sieges and the AI's military planning at once.
properties.name: OPEN — feudal service instead of wages: knights owe you days, not hours

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. A measurement that raises a design question, found while keeping `draftHarshness` from the doctrine experiment.

WHAT WAS MEASURED, 8 games x 120 turns, personalities rotated across seats. `draftHarshness` replaced a hardcoded 0.5 that every ruler shared. Comparing against that shared-0.5 baseline:

  Knight    0.5 -> 0.8 (harsher):  28.3 -> 20.3 counties, 468 -> 383 soldiers
  Baron     0.5 -> 0.5 (unchanged): 30.3 -> 30.5 counties
  Countess  0.5 -> 0.45 (gentler):  40.3 -> 48.0 counties

All three moved in the direction their trait moved, which is why this reads as signal rather than noise: the gentler drafter gained, the harsher drafter lost, the unchanged one stayed put.

WHY IT HAPPENS, and it is coherent rather than a bug. Conscription costs happiness. Lower happiness means more emigration, more revolts, slower population growth and less production — so a harsher draft buys men now at the cost of the county that produces men later. The extra soldiers do not repay it.

THE DESIGN QUESTION. The manual gives the Knight his temperament: he works his peasantry "to the point of cruelty". Making that mechanical turns his characterisation into a straight penalty, and flavour that only ever costs you is a poor kind of flavour. Options, none decided:
(a) LEAVE IT. Harsh rule being self-defeating is a real and defensible thing for this game to say, and the Knight is meant to be reckless rather than optimal.
(b) GIVE HARSHNESS A COMPENSATION so it is a trade rather than a tax — the drafted men are better, or cheaper, or available faster, so a ruler in a hurry has a reason to be cruel.
(c) MODERATE THE NUMBER, keeping the flavour visible without the drag.

⚠️ THE HONEST LIMIT ON THE EVIDENCE: eight games. The effect is large and directionally consistent across three personalities, which is suggestive, but this is not the twenty-game baseline and should not be treated as settled. The standard baseline did not move at all (3/20 decided, 72 sieges laid, unchanged), so whatever this is, it is a per-ruler effect rather than a systemic one.

NOTE THE BISHOP IS ABSENT from these numbers entirely — he holds 0 counties in every game, eliminated early, because his aggression of 0.2 falls under the 0.3 gate that dec:idea-aggression-is-a-switch describes. He is not playing at all, which makes any comparison involving him meaningless until that is fixed.
properties.name: OPEN — drafting harder makes a ruler weaker, so the Knight's own flavour penalises him
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-28 immediately after measuring it, because the finding contradicts the intuition that drafting harder makes a ruler stronger, and because it turns a piece of the manual's own characterisation into a mechanical penalty — which is a design choice somebody should make on purpose rather than inherit.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-26 while making medieval economics more accurate.

THE MEDIEVAL FACT. Scholastic economics held that a good has a *justum pretium* — a just price — and that charging beyond it was sinful, not shrewd. This was not a sentiment but law and enforcement: assizes of bread and ale fixed prices for staples in England from the thirteenth century, forestalling and regrating (buying up supply to resell dear) were prosecutable offences, and a merchant who profiteered during a dearth could expect the pillory as readily as a profit. Adam Smith is five centuries away; the market here is a moral institution before it is a price-discovery mechanism.

WHY IT MATTERS RIGHT NOW. Supply-and-demand pricing has just gone in, and it works: grain fetches 1 crown in a glutted county and 7 in a starving one. Mechanically that is correct and it made trade a real decision. But it also means the most profitable act available to a ruler is to carry grain into a famine and sell it dear — and in the thirteenth century that is precisely the act that got men hanged. The game currently rewards it with no comment.

THE IDEA. Give the price a moral ceiling as well as an economic one. Selling into a shortage above some multiple of the base price angers the county it happens in and stains the seller's name — a happiness hit where it occurs, and a standing with the other nobles that suffers, since the existing diplomacy system already models reputation. Conversely, selling cheap into a famine, or shipping grain to a starving county of your own, is the medieval definition of good lordship and could earn what conquest cannot.

WHY IT FITS THIS GAME PARTICULARLY. Happiness and opinion already exist, tested and working; this needs no new machinery, only a consequence attached to a number the market already computes. It also closes the loop the playtest opened: the market now has an economic brake (the merchant's purse) but no moral one.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It punishes the player for playing the market the game just taught them to play, so it wants to be legible before it bites — a warning, not a silent penalty.
The manual says nothing about any of this; it is medieval accuracy, not Lords of the Realm II accuracy, and those are now demonstrably different targets.
And it cuts against the supply pricing that was just built and verified — deliberately, but the tension is real and should be tuned rather than assumed.

COST. Small. A threshold on the supply factor, a happiness delta, an opinion delta.
properties.name: OPEN — the just price: should profiteering in a famine cost you?

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Distinct from dec:idea-rulers-from-history: that asks whether to ground the rulers in history at all and which ones. This is about the specific choice the user named first, what it would mean mechanically, and the date problem it carries.

THE USER'S IDEA: "the knight could be based on Machiavelli 'the prince' and uses principles taught in that book."

THE DATE, stated because it should be a deliberate choice rather than an accident: THE PRINCE is 1513, Florentine, and the game sits in 1268 Britain — two and a half centuries and a different world. Machiavelli is not a ruler of this era; he is arguing against the political tradition that IS this era.

AND THAT IS THE BEST ARGUMENT FOR KEEPING HIM. The Prince was written as a deliberate rebuttal of the mirror-for-princes genre — the Aquinas/Giles of Rome tradition that says a king rules for the common good and a tyrant forfeits obedience. So a table where three rulers hold period doctrine and the Knight holds Machiavelli is not a research slip: it is the Knight playing by rules the others consider dishonourable, which is exactly the dramatic shape the user's "war-loving Knight who refuses alliances" already has in the code. The anachronism becomes the characterisation. The alternative, if the date should be clean, is Giles of Rome or Vegetius for a period-correct hard-headedness — cheaper to justify, duller to play against.

WHAT THE PRINCE ACTUALLY SAYS THAT THIS GAME CAN EXPRESS — and it is more than usual, because Machiavelli wrote about exactly the problems this simulation models:
- MERCENARIES ARE "disunited, ambitious, without discipline, unfaithful" and a prince should use his own arms. The game HAS mercenaries, with a gold cost and a wage multiplier, and the AI hires them when conscription cannot keep pace. A Machiavellian Knight simply refuses them — cheap to implement, unmistakable in play, and straight from the text.
- CRUELTIES SHOULD BE DONE ALL AT ONCE, benefits doled out little by little. Maps onto conquest: crush a taken county hard and immediately rather than grind it over seasons.
- EXTINGUISH THE LINE of the displaced ruler. Maps onto the capitulation rules just built: a Machiavellian ruler pursues elimination where another would accept a surrender.
- THE BEST FORTRESS IS NOT TO BE HATED. Maps onto the castle-versus-happiness spending choice — and it cuts AGAINST the war-loving reading, which is the interesting part.
- AVOID BEING HATED: do not touch subjects' property. Maps onto a tax ceiling he will not cross even when he can.

⚠️ THE COUNTER WORTH KEEPING: The Prince is a rhetorical and much-argued text, not a rulebook, and "Machiavellian" in popular use means something cruder than what Machiavelli wrote. A version built on the cartoon — betray everyone, tax everything — would be both bad history and a worse opponent than the careful thing the text actually describes. If this is built, the mercenary rule and the tax ceiling are the honest core; treachery-for-its-own-sake is the failure mode.

A SECOND COUNTER: it inherits the gating problem from dec:idea-rulers-from-history. None of these opinions is visible while traits are read as a single threshold.
properties.name: OPEN — the Knight plays The Prince, and is deliberately two centuries out of place
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-28. Recorded separately because the date problem has a real answer that changes the idea rather than killing it, and because the mercenary rule is a concrete, cheap, textually faithful mechanic that could be tried on its own.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-26.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW, precisely. Industry is `output = min(workers x rate, tileCapacity)` — dead linear in headcount until it hits a hard per-tile ceiling, then flat. Agriculture is the same shape: `min(1, workers / needed)`. So the hundredth miner produces exactly as much as the first, right up to a cliff where the hundred-and-first produces nothing at all. Ajs described the original as linear to a 999-ton cap; this remake has the same shape with a smaller ceiling.

⚠️ AND NOTHING IS SKILLED. Workers are interchangeable and instantly productive. Move the whole county into the mine this season and out again next season and nothing is lost.

THE IDEA. Replace the cliff with a curve — each additional worker adds less than the last, so a mine reaches a natural practical limit long before any hard cap. Ajs: "after a certain point, you don't increase productivity by adding another worker."

WHY IT IS MORE THAN REALISM. It makes the labour slider a real decision every season. Under linear-to-a-cliff the optimum is trivially computable and static: fill each task to exactly its cap. Under diminishing returns the last few workers in the mine are always worth less than the first few in the fields, so moving hands to the harvest and back is correct play rather than fiddling — which is exactly the seasonal rhythm Ajs was reaching for, and which Advanced Farming's seasonal grain demand already half-implements.

THE SKILL HALF, and Ajs flagged his own uncertainty here: something like four seasons for a worker to reach full output at a mine, after which keeping ONE trained hand there preserves the skill and the rest can come and go freely. He added "that isn't quite right", so the mechanic is a sketch rather than a spec. What is worth keeping from it is the PRINCIPLE: skill lives in the workplace rather than in the worker, so abandoning a mine entirely costs you something that shuffling hands does not. Historically that is roughly true — mining and smithing were craft trades where a core of experienced men carried the knowledge and casual labour did the hauling.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
Diminishing returns interacts with the equal-division labour model: workers currently split evenly among tasks that need work, so nobody is choosing where the marginal worker goes. A curve is only meaningful if allocation can respond to it.
The skill layer adds per-county, per-industry state that must be saved, and its main risk is being invisible — a player who cannot see why a mine is producing badly will read it as a bug.
And this is balance work on numbers the README already calls placeholders, with no harness to say whether the result is better.

COST. The curve is small: one function, and it replaces a min() that already exists. The skill layer is medium and wants UI to be legible at all.
properties.name: OPEN — diminishing returns and skilled labour, instead of linear-then-a-cliff

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From reading the Lords of the Realm II manual end to end on 2026-08-26, after Ajs said "when I first tried playing the game, it didn't seem to work" and asked to get closer to the vibe of the inspiration.

THE MANUAL'S GAME, IN ITS OWN WORDS. The year is 1268, the King is dead without an heir, and several nobles contest the crown. "You begin the game with a SINGLE county. With its meager resources, you must build a large following, a successful economy and, ultimately, a powerful army." Each turn is a season, and there are six things a player does: manage counties (feed, allocate labour between food and industry, watch the treasury, BUY AND SELL AT A VISITING MERCHANT'S WAGON, send supplies, check castle progress); create and dispatch armies; build castles; fight battles and sieges; conduct diplomacy; end the turn.

WHERE THIS GAME DIFFERS — the vibe gaps, biggest first.

1. YOU START WITH THREE COUNTIES, NOT ONE. Every noble in the roster begins with a home cluster of three. The manual's whole arc is scrabbling up from one county with meagre resources, and starting with three deletes the early game — the part where the economy actually matters.

2. THERE IS NO MARKETPLACE. The manual's merchant wagon travels a route between counties, visiting a central county almost every season and a remote one rarely, and trades cows, ale, grain, stone, wood, iron, pikes, maces, swords, bows, crossbows and knights' mail, with a deliberate spread between buying and selling prices. This game has only BuyAle; commands/types.ts still lists "merchant Buy/Sell" as a FUTURE command. The consequence is visible within a few turns of play: gold and materials pile up with nothing to spend them on, and a surplus of grain cannot become anything else. It is the economy's only sink and its only source of what a county cannot produce.

3. THE PLAYER HAS NO IDENTITY. The manual: "you will be prompted to enter your name and choose a shield that will be your coat of arms. The shield's colour will serve as your identifying colour throughout the game." Here the player is called "You" and picks nothing.

4. THE RIVAL NOBLES ARE NOT THE MANUAL'S. The manual's opponents are the Bishop, the Baron, the Knight and the Countess, each with a profile and a temperament. The code models those personalities faithfully but names the characters The Bruce, Llywelyn, Earl of York and De Warenne. Whether to use the manual's four or keep historical Britons is a taste question, not a defect.

5. NOTHING TEACHES THE GAME. The manual leans on tip screens that appear automatically and tooltips on every button, both toggleable. This game has neither, and the new-game setup form sits permanently in the HUD during play, which reads as a debug panel rather than a game.

6. BATTLES ARE AUTO-RESOLVED. The manual gives real-time tactical battles eight pages — pause, issue orders, unit selection. The core README records auto-resolution as a deliberate choice, so this is noted as a known divergence rather than a gap, but it is the single largest difference in what playing feels like.

7. NO PILLAGING, which the manual carries as its own section.

SEPARATELY, TWO CONCRETE DEFECTS FOUND BY PLAYING, not vibe questions — see the linked findings.
properties.name: OPEN — what the manual says the game is, and where this one differs
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-26 from a full read of the manual plus a scripted play session. Recorded as an open question rather than as intent because it is a menu of possible work, and which parts matter is Ajs's call.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. This one is NOT Ajs's idea — it came out of reading the manual he pointed at, and it is recorded because it bears directly on the map question he did raise. Ajs said: "probably need to review the manual to determine /req for the game play."

WHAT THE MANUAL SHOWS (pages 20-22). The original has TWO map scales, and the current game has one.
- The MAIN MAP is zoomed in: an isometric view of a portion of the realm showing individual fields, the county town growing from a settlement into a walled town as the county prospers, roads, county borders drawn as stone walls, grazing cattle, merchant wagons, transport wagons and armies. The selected county is always the one in the centre of the view.
- The OVERVIEW MAP is the whole realm at once — "England Circa AD 1268" — showing every county, plus armies, merchants, castles, supply wagons and revolting peasants. Counties are irregular painted regions with visible borders, and the silhouette reads unmistakably as England.
- A MINI MAP sits in the control panel with colour-coded overlays for idle serfs, rations and happiness per county.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: the two scales are what let the original be both a management game and a map game. Fields are visible because labour allocation is about fields. If counties become genuinely multi-tile at real resolution, the tiles are the natural place for the main map's detail to live — worked fields, the county town, roads — and the map-shape question quietly decides how much of this is reachable later.

TWO PARTS, COUPLED.
(1) Two scales or one? The current SVG map with zoom does part of the overview map's job already, and the HUD's realm overview does part of the mini map's. A true zoomed-in county view is new UI.
(2) How much within-county detail? The design already renders settlements scaled by population and worked farm tiles, so some of this exists. County towns that visibly grow, roads and visible wagons do not.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: this is the largest scope idea in the set and none of it was asked for. The original had a full-time art team and a 1996 budget; the current game reached playable by making the map DOM/SVG and testable rather than pretty. Two map scales roughly doubles the client's UI surface, and the recorded quality target for this project is maintainability. It is entirely reasonable to answer this "one scale, and the overview is the one worth having" and stop.
properties.name: OPEN — how much of the original's two-scale map presentation do we want?
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-26 while reviewing the manual Ajs pointed at. Recorded as an idea beside his, explicitly attributed as not his, so a later session does not read it as something he asked for.

properties.decision:
SETTLED by Ajs on 2026-08-26: "go with the rasterised coastline approach" — option (b) of the four weighed below.

THE CHOSEN APPROACH. A real, low-resolution outline of Great Britain is rasterised onto the hex grid as a LAND MASK. A hex is land because the coastline says so, not because it falls within a radius of a county centre. Land hexes are then assigned to their nearest county centre, so counties remain Voronoi-shaped but only ever within a true coast. Sea stays sea.

WHY THIS ONE. It is the smallest change that actually fixes the complaint. The problem was never that counties were single hexes — they were already multi-hex blobs — but that the island's SILHOUETTE was derived from where ~90 hand-placed county centres sat, making it a union of circles. Rasterising inverts the dependency: geography decides the coast, and counties fill it.

IT SUBSUMES THE CHEAP OPTION RATHER THAN DISCARDING IT. Resolution must rise too — F=2 gives roughly five hexes per county, far too coarse for a coastline to be expressible at all. So raising F is part of this work, not an alternative to it. That matters: on its own, raising F was the option that looked like progress and fixed nothing.

WHY NOT THE OTHERS. Fully authored tile files plus a map editor (option c) and the hybrid (option d) were both rejected as disproportionate once Britain-only was settled in the same breath: with one map, a file format and an editor have nothing to amortise against. Recorded so a later reader knows they were weighed, not overlooked — and if a second map is ever wanted, option (d) is the one to revisit.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DECIDE, AND IS NOW THE NEXT REAL QUESTION: where the coastline data comes from, and under what licence. This project's own policy is strict — original content only, no original-game assets, output of the extraction tools gitignored — and the codebase is GPL-3.0-or-later. Real-world geography is fact and not copyrightable, but a specific dataset carries its own terms. Natural Earth is public domain and ships 1:10m and 1:50m coastlines, which is the obvious safe source; OpenStreetMap coastline data is ODbL, which brings attribution and share-alike obligations that would have to be honoured deliberately rather than by accident.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT FROM THE ORIGINAL BRAINSTORM STILL STANDS, and is now work rather than warning: county adjacency is hand-declared in britain.ts with a connectivity test guarding it, and ferry links exist precisely because tile pathfinding is land-only. A real coastline invalidates both until they are re-derived or re-authored, and every distance in the game changes at once when resolution rises, so movement speeds and siege and convoy pacing need retuning. The cost is in the systems downstream of the map, not in the map.
properties.name: Rasterise a real coastline as a land mask, then assign land to counties
properties.rationale: Ajs chose this on 2026-08-26 after the four options were weighed, together with Britain-only — which is what makes it proportionate. The diagnosis that drove the choice (the coastline was derived, not authored) came from reading britain-tiles.ts during the brainstorm.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list: Civilization V.

THE PROBLEM IT ANSWERS. Most of the map is neutral — 82 counties, and in a three-noble game only nine of them belong to anybody. Those seventy-odd counties are inert scenery: they have populations, farms and happiness, but no will. They cannot be talked to, bribed, allied with or provoked; they can only be walked into. The early game is therefore a land grab against no opposition, which is a large part of why the first several turns feel like nothing is happening.

THE IDEA. Give neutral counties a minor lord with an opinion of you, in the manner of Civ V's city-states. Then the whole existing diplomacy system — gifts, compliments, insults, alliances, opinion decay, the red/blue/green bands — points at them. You could buy a county's loyalty with gold instead of blood, be refused, be played off against a rival who is bidding for the same county, or find that the shire you have been bullying opens its gates to your enemy.

WHY IT IS CHEAPER THAN IT SOUNDS. Diplomacy is already built, tested and working — opinion, alliance, betrayal and decay all exist. The addition is actors to point it at, not machinery.

⚠️ COUNTER, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL. Victory is "last realm standing". Modelling seventy minor lords as realms would break that immediately — the game could never end. It would need either one shared "Independent" realm holding every neutral county, which is cheap but makes them all move as a bloc, or a minor-lord actor that is deliberately NOT a realm and is therefore invisible to the elimination and victory checks. The second is right and is the more delicate change: conquest, elimination and outcome all currently reason in terms of realms.

SECOND COUNTER: it competes directly with the manual's own answer. The manual's neutral counties are simply unclaimed, and the drama is meant to come from the four rival nobles. This is the least faithful idea in the set after a tech tree — worth wanting anyway, but worth knowing.

COST. Medium, and mostly in the victory and elimination logic rather than in the diplomacy.
properties.name: OPEN — should neutral counties be living minor lords rather than empty land? (Civ V city-states)

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. What remains after garrison-on-capture fixed conquest permanence on 2026-08-27, measured rather than guessed.

WHAT THE PERMANENCE FIX SETTLED. Garrisoned counties went from three of eighty to seventy-four of seventy-five. A realm's interior is now solid and land has to be taken from somebody. That part is done.

WHAT IT REVEALED UNDERNEATH. Still no game decided, at 200 turns or at 500 — a hundred and twenty-five years. At 500 turns there were 115 sieges WON across only 26 counties ever besieged, so each contested county changed hands four or five times. The interior is stable; the FRONTIER is a meat grinder. Two powers settle at roughly forty percent of the map each and grind.

THE MECHANISM. An offensive takes a county, spends men garrisoning it, is weaker for the next siege, and stalls — then the defender does the same in reverse. Attrition equalises at the front by construction. And the AI reinforces only armies standing on FRIENDLY soil, so a host deep in enemy territory can never be topped up: every offensive is a one-shot with a shrinking magazine.

FOUR THINGS THAT MIGHT BREAK A FRONT, none chosen.

(a) LET AN ARMY BE REINFORCED IN THE FIELD, at a price. Supply convoys already carry food to an army in enemy territory; men could travel the same way. This is the smallest change and it targets the mechanism directly.

(b) LET GARRISONS COME FROM THE COUNTY, NOT THE ARMY. A conquered population can be made to watch its own gate, so holding land stops draining the field army. Historically shakier — an occupier does not usually arm the conquered — but it removes the attrition without removing the permanence.

(c) MAKE THE AI CONCENTRATE. Several small hosts grinding separately is the worst possible use of the same men; one large one might break through. This is planning, not rules, and would not change a human's game at all.

(d) ACCEPT A LONGER WAR AND END IT ANOTHER WAY. Victory only by total conquest is an accepted decision, but a fifty-year stalemate between two great powers is arguably a historically honest outcome that the VICTORY CONDITION, not the war, is failing to recognise. A crown claimed by holding most of the realm for long enough would end these games — at the cost of reopening a decision already taken.

⚠️ COUNTER TO ALL OF IT. Zero deserters in every game means armies are not limited by cost at all, so any change that simply makes armies bigger will be absorbed without being felt. Whatever is tried should be measured on the same twenty seeds, which is now a two-minute job rather than an argument.
properties.name: OPEN — offensives cannot be sustained, so the front grinds forever

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent; it is an open question with options.

The user's thought, in their words: "so often gaming is limited to what objects the game defines for you and you using them in the game. What if the user was able to define its own 'class' with attributes and the AI populated the game object. For instance, say the user said I want to develop a new logistics strategy or a new defense against Viking raids by putting blocks in a river. The user would provide the concept to the AI, the AI would extract/parse content from it, then populate the game object which could then be used as a game element. Maybe don't make every game element, but start with a few that could be tailored by the user."

Options as they stand:
(a) FILL-A-STRUCT — the LLM only fills in a typed slot the sim already has: name, cost, build time, effect magnitude, the county it sits in. The sim validates and clamps. Cheapest by a wide margin; the rules engine changes not at all.
(b) FILL-A-STRUCT PLUS A HOOK — the LLM fills a struct AND names which existing generic hook the object attaches to (a river-edge movement modifier, a supply-route interdiction, a per-county happiness modifier). Requires the sim to grow a small number of named, generic attachment points first. Medium.
(c) THE LLM WRITES RULES — it emits behaviour, not data. Much larger, and a different project: it is code generation inside a deterministic core.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT WORTH KEEPING, and it is the load-bearing one: an LLM can only fill in shapes the sim already has a hole for. "Blocks in a river" is only expressible if movement already supports a per-edge modifier that something can attach to. If that hook does not exist, no amount of parsing produces it — the model would have to write and load code, which is option (c). So the real work of this idea is NOT the LLM; it is deciding which generic hooks the simulation exposes. The LLM is the cheap half. That reframing is a finding, not a verdict.

A DISTINCTION THE QUESTION HAS TO RESOLVE: the two examples given are not the same kind of thing. "A defense against Viking raids by putting blocks in a river" is an OBJECT — a thing that exists at a place with attributes. "A new logistics strategy" is a POLICY — a standing doctrine that changes how existing objects behave over time. Objects are far cheaper (they fit (a)/(b)); policies need a rules interpreter or a standing-orders system that does not exist yet.

A SECOND COUNTER-ARGUMENT: the fun may be in the writing, not the playing. A player-authored object that the sim reduces to "+15% defence on river tiles" can feel like a lot of typing for a number. Whether the invention reads as invention, or as a slow way to pick a modifier, is the thing that decides if this is worth building — and it is testable cheaply with a paper mock before any LLM is wired in.
properties.name: OPEN — the player defines its own class, and the AI populates the game object

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list: Civilization V.

THE PROBLEM IT ANSWERS, AND IT IS THE BIGGEST STRUCTURAL ONE IN THE SET. This game has no progression whatsoever. The units you can build in year 1 are the units you can build in year 40; the buildings, the castle types, the farming methods and the weapons are all available from the first season, gated only by materials. Nothing is ever unlocked, so nothing is ever looked forward to. Civ V's answer is eras and a tech tree: the shape of the game changes underneath you, and a long game is long because it keeps becoming a different game.

WHAT IT COULD LOOK LIKE HERE, WITHOUT A SCIENCE SCREEN. The medieval frame supplies its own progression and none of it needs a laboratory: the three-field rotation arriving as an improvement over two-field; the heavy plough; the transition from motte-and-bailey to stone keep to concentric castle (the castle types ALREADY EXIST as a ladder and are gated only by cost); crossbow then plate then the longbow; the wool trade. Progress could be bought with gold and time rather than researched, which suits a game about a treasury rather than a civilisation.

⚠️ COUNTER, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST OBJECTION TO ANY IDEA HERE. The manual has no technology of any kind, and this project's first stated goal is a faithful remake before new features. A tech spine is the single least faithful thing on this list. It is also the largest: progression is not a system beside the others, it is a modifier on ALL of them — production, combat, castles, farming, conscription — and the project's recorded quality target is maintainability, meaning things that change together should live together. A tech tree changes together with everything.

A CHEAPER VERSION THAT KEEPS MOST OF THE FEELING: no tree at all, just a small number of era thresholds tied to the calendar or to realm size, each unlocking one or two things that already exist in the code but are currently always available. That is a gate on existing content rather than new content, and it is a fraction of the work.

COST. Full tech tree: the largest item in this brainstorm by a wide margin. Era gates on existing content: small.
