properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-27, from looking at how each successive conqueror of Britain solved the same problem.

THE HISTORICAL FACT. Rome's answer to logistics was not better wagons, it was INFRASTRUCTURE. Something like two thousand miles of engineered road went into Britain — Watling Street, Ermine Street, the Fosse Way — laid straight, drained, metalled, and built by the army for the army. A road is how you double the radius at which a cart still arrives with something in it, and it is why the Roman conquest advanced the way it did: road by road, fort by fort, each one making the next stretch supportable. The roads outlasted the empire by a thousand years and every later invader used them, which is its own argument for what they were worth. The Normans and the medieval English inherited a network they could not have built.

THE IDEA. Roads as something a ruler BUILDS, between counties, consuming stone and timber and labour. A road makes supply cheaper along it and marching faster, so the wagon's radius stretches where you have invested and stays short where you have not.

WHY IT IS THE STRONGEST IDEA IN THIS SET: IT ANSWERS THREE OPEN PROBLEMS AT ONCE.
It gives the wagon radius something a player can DO about it — otherwise supply range is a wall you discover rather than a problem you solve, which is much less interesting.
It gives timber and stone a continuous sink, and the balance harness measured a leader ending with 180,000 units of materials that nothing consumes. Castles are a one-per-county sink that saturates; a road network never does.
And it makes conquest cumulative rather than a raid: a realm that has built roads into a frontier can sustain an offensive there, which is exactly what the measured stalemate lacks.

The manual also shows roads on the main map, so this is source material as well as history — one more of its systems that was never built.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It is the most CONTENT of the logistics ideas: an edge-built thing between counties, with construction, cost, upkeep, a UI to order it and something on the map to show it. Bigger than the wagon by a good margin.
It also risks making the early game a road-building simulator, and a realm that turtles and builds roads for twenty years while nobody attacks it would be playing correctly, which may not be the game anyone wants.
And roads help whoever uses them — including the invader. That is historically exact, it is exactly why the Roman network mattered to everyone who came after, and it makes building one a genuine gamble rather than a free improvement.

COST. Medium to large, and the largest thing here after river supply. But it is the one whose payoff reaches furthest outside logistics.
properties.name: OPEN — roads: the Roman answer, and the one idea that fixes three problems at once

The user's thought, 2026-08-28: "I was thinking we could base some of the other characters off politicians and rulers of the time. I was thinking the knight could be based on Machiavelli 'the prince' and uses principles taught in that book. maybe we could base the other PC controlled players off other rulers/monarchs of the era? then their play is based/influenced on how rulers of the time would have ruled/conquered."

DISTINCT FROM dec:idea-asymmetric-houses, which asks whether the four HOUSES should give the PLAYER different economies and combat. This asks what the AI BELIEVES — the doctrine behind its choices. The two compose (a house could play differently and be run on a doctrine) and either could be built without the other.

THE PERIOD IS BETTER STOCKED THAN IT LOOKS, and it answers the "rulers of the era" instinct directly. The game sits in 1268 Britain, and that is almost exactly the moment of Aquinas's DE REGNO (c. 1267) — a mirror-for-princes arguing the king rules for the common good and that a tyrant forfeits obedience. Giles of Rome's DE REGIMINE PRINCIPUM (1280) is the same genre and was the most-copied political text of the age; Vegetius's DE RE MILITARI was the campaign manual every commander actually read; John of Salisbury's POLICRATICUS (1159) had already justified tyrannicide. Contemporary rulers give the same spread with faces on: EDWARD I, whose answer to conquest was the iron ring of Welsh castles and who took ground methodically and fortified everything; ROBERT THE BRUCE, who did the opposite a generation later — refused the set-piece battle and SLIGHTED castles rather than garrison them; SIMON DE MONTFORT, dead in 1265, who fought the crown by building a baronial coalition and summoning a parliament; LLYWELYN AP GRUFFUDD, holding out on terrain nobody else wanted to fight on.

WHAT MAKES THIS MORE THAN A RENAME. Each of those is already a strategy this game can express: fortify-everything versus deny-the-enemy-strongpoints is a real fork in a game with castles and sieges; coalition-building is the diplomacy system; terrain-holding is the movement and supply system. The doctrines are not decoration on top of the mechanics, they are opinions ABOUT the mechanics that already exist.

COST, three tiers and the middle one is the interesting one.
(a) REFLAVOUR — names, portraits, a line of quoted doctrine per ruler. Pure text, no mechanics. Cheapest by far, and it will read as a rename because it IS one.
(b) DOCTRINE AS WEIGHTS — each ruler carries opinions the existing planners read: will he hire mercenaries, how high will he tax, does he spend on walls or on winning the people over, does he pursue a beaten rival to extinction or take a surrender. Every one of those maps onto a system already in the code. Medium, and the honest version.
(c) DISTINCT DECISION PROCEDURES — a separate planner per ruler. Large, and it multiplies the AI surface by four with no balance harness able to tell four AIs apart yet.

⚠️ THE LOAD-BEARING COUNTER, and it is measured rather than theoretical: personality barely drives anything today. dec:idea-aggression-is-a-switch records that `traits.aggression` is read in exactly two places in the whole AI and both read it as `< 0.3` — a single threshold, not a degree. Ten games at aggression 1 against ten at aggression 3 on the same seeds gave identical medians. So a doctrine layer built on top of today's traits would be invisible: four rulers with four philosophies and one behaviour. THIS IDEA IS GATED ON THE TRAITS BECOMING REAL LEVERS FIRST — which is also an argument FOR doing that work, since it gives the dial a reason to exist.

A SECOND COUNTER, from dec:idea-asymmetric-houses and it applies here too: this is small in code and large in balancing. Four doctrines is four things to balance, with a harness that currently cannot tell whether a change helped.

AN UNTESTED HOPE, flagged as such: the baseline shows the eventual winner leading from turn 0 in every one of twenty games — there is no comeback in this design. Genuinely different doctrines might create the counter-play that produces one. That is speculation and should not be used to justify the work.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list of games worth stealing from: Settlers of Catan.

THE IDEA. Catan's whole engine is that you cannot get what you need on your own. Resources are unevenly spread, nobody is self-sufficient, and every turn is spent working out who has the wood you need and what they will take for it. Ported here: counties already sit on uneven ground — wheat, pasture, wood, stone, iron and fish are scattered by terrain across 82 counties — so a realm holding the Weald has timber and no iron, and one holding the Pennines has the reverse. Trade with the merchant, and with rival nobles, becomes the way you fix that.

WHY IT FITS. The map already generates the scarcity; nothing consumes it. And it lands exactly on the biggest hole the manual reading found: there is no marketplace, so gold and materials pile up with nothing to spend them on.

⚠️ THE CATCH, AND IT IS A REAL ONE. The realm has ONE SHARED TREASURY. The manual states it outright: "they all share one treasury and all the items in it. When one of your counties produces or buys stone, for example, the stone immediately becomes available to all the other counties in your realm." So the moment you hold two counties, scarcity dissolves — one iron county supplies the realm forever, and there is nothing to trade for. Catan-style scarcity and the shared treasury cannot both be true. Making this idea bite means either breaking a feature the manual explicitly describes, or finding the scarcity somewhere else: per-county stockpiles with a transport cost, or scarcity in TIME (you have iron, but not this season, and the smith is idle) rather than in kind.

COST. Cheap once a marketplace exists; near-worthless before one. The marketplace is the prerequisite, not this.

WHAT NOT TO TAKE FROM CATAN. Dice-driven tile yields would collide with the weather and fertility system already built for that job. Victory points — longest road, largest army — contradict the accepted decision that the game is won only by total conquest.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-27 while looking at how logistics decided medieval sieges.

THE HISTORICAL FACT, and it is the one most games get backwards. A siege was usually more dangerous to the ARMY OUTSIDE the walls than to the garrison inside. The besieger sits still in one place, eats out the surrounding country within weeks, and then must be supplied from elsewhere or starve — while camped in his own filth. At Antioch in 1097-98 the besieging crusaders starved, ate their horses, and deserted in numbers before the city fell. Henry V lost perhaps a third of his army to dysentery at HARFLEUR in 1415 and fought Agincourt with the sick remnant. Countless sieges simply dissolved because the attacking army did.

WHAT THE GAME DOES NOW. Foraging already draws an army's food from the county it occupies, so a besieger does strip the land it sits on and can starve — the mechanism is there. What is missing is the second killer: nothing represents the camp itself. A besieging army takes no losses from sitting still in one place for six seasons, and disease is the largest cause of medieval military death by a wide margin.

THE IDEA. A besieging army suffers attrition that grows with how long it has sat and how thoroughly it has stripped the county under it — sickness in the lines, desertion, horses eaten. The besieger is racing the garrison's larder against his own, which is exactly the tension a medieval siege had and the game currently lacks: right now a siege is a timer the attacker cannot lose.

WHY IT MIGHT ALSO HELP THE STALL. The harness found a frontier where sieges are won 115 times across 26 counties — an endless mutual grinding. Making a siege genuinely costly to attempt would mean fewer, more deliberate sieges, and would push a ruler toward taking a weakly-held county rather than butting at a strong one. Fewer, better-chosen sieges is a healthier shape than many pointless ones.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It makes taking fortified ground HARDER, and fortified ground is already nearly untakeable — this could deepen the stalemate rather than break it. It probably only works alongside something that makes offensives sustainable.
Disease is also the least fun mechanic in most games that have it: losses to nothing, decided by a number the player cannot see or influence. It wants to be visible and answerable — better supply, a shorter siege, lifting and coming back — or it is just a tax on trying.

COST. Small. A per-season attrition on besieging armies, keyed to seasons elapsed and the county's remaining stores, both of which the siege system already tracks.
properties.name: OPEN — the siege consumes the besieger: camp disease and a stripped countryside

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL, and it is my push-back rather than Ajs's idea. Raised 2026-08-27.

THE COMPLAINT WAS NOT ACTUALLY ABOUT VARIETY. Ajs's words: "I knew exactly how to defeat each castle type and how to protect them — so it became predictable and mechanical of just doing the same thing each time." The failure there is not that there were only five designs. It is that the player had PERFECT INFORMATION and NO COMMITMENT COST, so the optimal answer could be computed once and replayed forever. Give that same player fifty designable features and full visibility and they will build a bigger lookup table and go on playing mechanically. Variety without uncertainty is more homework, not more game.

WHAT ACTUALLY MAKES A SIEGE A DECISION. Two things, and the game already half has both.
YOU MUST COMMIT BEFORE YOU KNOW. Siege engines already take SEASONS to build, and the manual is explicit that the bigger the army the faster they rise. If a besieger must choose which engines to raise before he knows whether the wall is thick or the foundations are rock, that choice is a wager rather than a calculation. Choosing wrong should mean seasons wasted and a repulsed assault, which the siege system already models.
AND KNOWING SHOULD COST SOMETHING. Scouting, a probing assault that reveals where the walls are weak, a bribed servant, the reports of merchants who have been inside. The exploration option already models a realm seeing only what it has been near, so there is a fog to build on.

HISTORICALLY THIS IS EXACT. Besiegers routinely did not know what they faced — Château Gaillard fell because the French found a chapel window nobody had reckoned on, and Philip's engineers spent months on the wrong approaches first. The mining tunnel that decided Rochester was a gamble that happened to come off.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
Hidden information can feel like arbitrary loss rather than a gamble taken. It only works if the player can see what they DID know, what they guessed, and what it cost — a siege that fails for reasons never revealed is just a dice roll with extra steps.
It also asks more of the AI than any other idea here: an AI that must reason about what it does not know is a genuinely harder thing to write than one comparing numbers, and a badly done one will simply always guess right or always guess wrong.
And it multiplies with the castle-design question rather than adding to it: designable castles plus imperfect information is where the interest is, but it is also two systems at once.
properties.name: OPEN — what a besieger is allowed to know, which is the real cure for predictability

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs, 2026-08-27: "there is probably some science to which castles survived and did well and which castles did poorly and were overcome." There is, and it is unusually well documented.

WHAT ACTUALLY DECIDED MEDIEVAL SIEGES.
MINING WAS THE GREAT WALL-KILLER. At Rochester in 1215 King John undermined the keep's south-east corner, propping the tunnel with timber and firing it with the fat of forty pigs; the corner came down. It was rebuilt ROUND, because a square corner is a mine's best friend and a round tower has no corner to take. Counter-mining was a real defence — at Dover in 1216 the English dug out to intercept Louis's tunnels.
WATER DEFEATED MINING OUTRIGHT. You cannot tunnel under a lake. Caerphilly's water defences are the largest in Britain and it was never taken by storm; Kenilworth held six months against Henry III in 1266 — trebuchets, siege towers, even barges — and was only starved out.
THE GATEHOUSE STOPPED BEING THE WEAK POINT and became the strongest, at Harlech and Caerphilly — a gatehouse-keep, so the obvious way in was the worst way in.
CONCENTRIC WALLS turned a breach into a trap: get through the outer at Beaumaris and you stand in a killing ground overlooked from the inner.
THE WELL decided more sieges than the engines did. A castle without water in the rock had a clock on it.
AND ONE WEAK ADDITION UNDOES EVERYTHING. Château Gaillard was Richard I's masterpiece and Philip II took it in about six months in 1203-04, the French getting into the middle bailey through a chapel that John had added — a window where there should have been wall.
Meanwhile HARLECH held in 1294-95 with a garrison of about thirty-seven men, because it could be resupplied by sea. Siting and supply beat thickness.

THE IDEA. Make each attack and each defence SPECIFIC, so no single answer works everywhere. Mining against foundations, defeated by rock siting, a wet moat, round towers, or counter-mining. Rams against gates, defeated by a barbican or a gatehouse-keep. Escalade against height, defeated by walls and hoardings. Bombardment against thickness. Starvation against the well and the granary — and against the besieger's own supply, which the logistics work has just made real.

WHY THIS IS THE HALF THAT ANSWERS AJS'S COMPLAINT. "I knew exactly how to defeat each castle type" is a symptom of ONE attack axis: today a siege is engines versus a defence multiplier, so there is exactly one way to attack and one number that resists it. Several axes, each answered by a different investment, means a castle can be strong and still have a way in — which is what made real sieges interesting.

⚠️ COUNTERS. Rock-paper-scissors solves too cleanly if the player can see the whole board — the information question recorded beside this one matters more than the number of axes. And every axis added is another thing to explain, another thing to build engines for, and another thing an AI has to reason about; four good axes will beat eight thin ones.
properties.name: OPEN — the science of what survived: specific attacks, specific counters

STILL RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — and NARROWED by Ajs on 2026-08-26, which is the part a later session must read before acting on the paragraphs below.

WHAT AJS ACTUALLY SETTLED. Asked whether to keep single-player-only as intent, he said: "We don't have to remove the single-player (but my preferred player mode is single player)." So: single-player is the mode he plays and the mode to design for, and multiplayer is NOT being retired. Nothing is dropped.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE DESIGN, CONCRETELY — the earlier framing in this node argued the opposite and was declined:
- "A clean frontend/backend split, eventually hosted online" STAYS accepted. It is unsatisfied, and it stays honestly unsatisfied, because nothing serves it since the REST service was retired. It is a standing goal, not dead weight.
- "The client holds no game rules" STAYS accepted, and the recorded violation against it is STILL a live finding. The client importing pathfinding, diplomacy predicates, the unit table and tile-map construction remains real debt, not something that dissolves. This is the practical consequence of not retiring multiplayer, and it is the one worth remembering.
- The two OBSOLETES edges this node once carried, asserting that confirming single-player would retire those two requirements, were DELETED once Ajs declined that consequence. They encoded a retirement that is not happening.

WHAT REMAINS TRUE AND UNCHANGED. Determinism and the plain-data GameState earn their keep regardless of player count — seeded RNG is what makes save/load resume exactly and the 168-case suite reproducible. That was recorded here as a risk when the question was framed as a retirement; with nothing being retired, the risk is smaller but the reasoning still holds: determinism should be justified on its own terms and not left leaning on the multiplayer goal.

WHAT IS STILL OPEN. Whether "preferred mode" ever hardens into "only mode". Until it does, features should not assume a single human player, but neither should effort go into hosted multiplayer that nothing is asking for.

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

The user's thought, raised 2026-08-28 while looking at the materials glut: "I experienced this in the original game where I kept piling up these indefinitely, which is unrealistic. Having 100000 tons of grain (somewhat perishable), 5 million tons of stone, etc just becomes unrealistic at some point (you couldn't possibly store it after a time). Basically, what I'm saying is there are limitations on how much capacity you have to store things."

WHAT PROMPTED IT, measured the same day: at turn 200 the leading realm held stone 119,377, wool 87,540, iron 58,472 and gold 112,975 — while wood sat at 12. Four of eleven traded goods were pinned at the price floor. Production outruns every sink and the surplus simply accumulates without limit.

Options, none decided:
(a) A HARD CAP PER STORE, probably tied to something the player builds or holds — county granaries and warehouses, or simply the number of counties. Production past the cap is wasted. Simplest to implement and the easiest to explain.
(b) SPOILAGE / DECAY, which the user's own words point at for grain ("somewhat perishable"). A percentage lost per season, perhaps different per good — grain rots, stone does not, iron rusts slowly. More realistic and it makes stockpiling a decision rather than a default, but it needs a rate per good and is easy to make annoying.
(c) BOTH, with capacity for bulk goods and spoilage for food.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND REALISM: a sink is exactly what the materials glut lacks, and it may bear on the decisiveness problem too. A realm that cannot hoard must spend — on castles, on armies, on trade — and the balance harness currently shows a leader sitting on six figures of materials while fielding two hundred and fifty men. Whether that connection is real is untested and should not be assumed.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT WORTH KEEPING: caps and spoilage both punish the player for succeeding, and a badly tuned version turns a strategy game into an inventory-management chore. The original game's unlimited piles were annoying but they were never the thing that made it boring. If this is built, the test is whether it creates an interesting decision (what do I build before the harvest rots?) or merely a tax.

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. The user's addition: "we can use the character extraction process from storyflow (which is a project on this machine) as template." Distinct from the other four — those ask whether to author objects, which slots, where the model runs, and how to price the result. This asks what the populate step is BUILT LIKE, and it would be the same question whichever way those go.

WHAT THE TEMPLATE ACTUALLY IS, read from /home/ajs/projects/storyflow/services/generation_plus/src/modules/extraction on 2026-08-27 (passes/characters.py, passes/_common.py, multi_pass_orchestrator.py):
- CLOSED VOCABULARY AXES. `CHARACTER_TYPES`, `CHARACTER_ROLES`, `INTERIORITY_MODES` are tuples declared in code, interpolated into the prompt, and the model must pick ONE value from each. The code owns the vocabulary; the model only chooses within it.
- A DECLARED JSON OUTPUT SHAPE written into the prompt, plus json_object mode on the API call.
- AN ERROR ENVELOPE THAT NEVER RAISES. `call_pass_llm` turns every failure — HTTP, connection, JSON decode, provider error — into a sentinel-keyed dict shaped by `default_keys`, so one bad pass cannot cascade into the others.
- CONTEXT INJECTION. `story_context` and `universe_context` carry what already exists into the prompt, so a new extraction is consistent with the established world rather than inventing a parallel one.
- DISAMBIGUATION RULES IN THE PROMPT. Long, specific instructions on aliases, hidden identities and possessive-determiner references exist purely to stop the model emitting near-duplicates of entities that already exist.
- MULTI-PASS LAYERING (P1/P2/P3 via asyncio.gather) with prefix-caching discipline, so parallel passes share a cached prose prefix.

WHY IT FITS: the closed-vocabulary axis is exactly the answer to the finding on dec:idea-player-authored-objects — that the model can only fill shapes the sim already has holes for. In storyflow, the enum IS the hole. Transferred here, the sim would declare its vocabulary (which hooks exist, which effects are expressible, what ranges are legal) and the model would only ever choose within it. The context-injection idea transfers just as directly: pass the county and realm state so an authored object fits the game in progress instead of inventing a parallel one. The never-raises envelope transfers too, and matters more here than there — a failed authoring call should leave the game untouched, not half-populated.

THE DIFFERENCE THAT MATTERS, and it is not a small one: storyflow's extraction is DESCRIPTIVE and this would be GENERATIVE. The characters are already in the prose; the model reports what is there, and a wrong answer is a misreading of a text anyone can check against. "Blocks in a river" contains no cost, no build time, no defence value — the model would be INVENTING numbers with balance consequences, not extracting facts. Extraction has a ground truth to be wrong about; authoring has none. So the machinery transfers cleanly and the VALIDATION STORY does not: storyflow can check output against the prose, and nothing here can check an authored object against anything until something prices it. That lands squarely back on dec:idea-authored-object-balance.

TWO SMALLER MISMATCHES: storyflow is a Python service calling OpenRouter over the network at temperature 0.3, and this project is a dependency-free deterministic TypeScript core with an offline requirement — so the pass would have to live wholly outside the sim core, which is the authoring-time-only shape already recorded on dec:idea-where-the-llm-runs. And the multi-pass P1/P2/P3 layering is almost certainly overkill for one small object; the cheap transfer is a single pass with closed vocabulary, a declared shape and the error envelope.

NOT TO BE CONFUSED WITH cmp:extract-tools / cap:original-data-extraction, which is a different thing sharing the word: pulling reference data out of the original game's files.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-27 — what the successive conquerors of Britain each did about holding ground.

TWO HISTORICAL ANSWERS TO THE SAME PROBLEM, and they are mirror images.

ALFRED'S BURHS were the defensive answer to fast raiders. From the 880s Wessex was fitted with a ring of fortified towns, garrisoned in rotation by an assessment recorded in the Burghal Hidage, and — the crucial part — SPACED so that nowhere in the kingdom was more than about twenty miles from one. That is a day's march. A Viking army could still land and still ride, but it could no longer move through Wessex without a garrison in reach of it, and it could no longer winter unmolested. The network beat the raiders, not any single fortress.

WILLIAM'S CASTLES were the offensive answer. After 1066 the Normans threw up motte-and-bailey castles at extraordinary speed — earth and timber, days rather than years, a prefabricated one carried over in the invasion fleet — and they placed them to CONTROL, at river crossings, road junctions and a ride apart. Several hundred within a generation. The castle was not where you retreated to; it was the instrument by which a few thousand Normans held a country of two million.

THE COMMON INSIGHT, and it is the one the game is missing. In both cases what mattered was not how strong any one place was but HOW THE PLACES RELATED TO EACH OTHER — spacing, mutual support, and the radius each one dominated. This game has castles as isolated buildings: a county either has one or it does not, and it defends only itself. Nothing represents a castle projecting control over the ground around it, or two garrisons within supporting distance being worth more than the same two far apart.

THE IDEA. Give a castle a radius of control, so a fortress makes the counties near it harder to raid, easier to supply, and quicker to reinforce — and so that castles sited to support one another are worth more than castles scattered. Conquest then becomes a matter of building a network forward, which is what it historically was.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It is the most abstract idea in this set: a radius of control is a game concept dressed in history, and unlike the wagon eating its load there is no clean arithmetic behind it — the numbers would be invented.
It would also make the map stickier at exactly the moment the harness says the map is already too sticky to break, so it needs to arrive with something that makes offensives possible, not before it.
And it partly overlaps garrison-on-capture, which just gave every taken county a holding force; the marginal value of a control radius on top of that is unproven.

COST. Medium. Castles, garrisons and county adjacency all exist; what is new is the relationship between them.
properties.name: OPEN — the burh and the motte: a network of strongpoints, not a scatter of castles

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. From Ajs's list: Risk, and Civilization V.

THE PROBLEM IT ANSWERS. Right now every county is worth the same as every other, and there is no reason to take THIS one rather than that one — nor any reason to stop. Conquest has a cost in men and gold but no structural brake, which is part of why an AI ruler can run to 21 counties by year 6 without anything pushing back.

TWO HALVES, PULLING OPPOSITE WAYS ON PURPOSE.

THE CARROT — Risk's continent bonus. Hold every county in a region and the whole region pays a premium. This is nearly free: MapRegion already carries `country`, so England, Wales and Scotland exist in the data today. It gives the map strategic shape — suddenly the last county in Wales is worth three ordinary ones.
⚠️ COUNTER: Britain has only three countries and they are wildly uneven — England is 39 counties, Scotland 30, Wales 13. A bonus for holding England is barely distinguishable from having already won, and Wales is a soft target that hands an early snowball to whoever starts nearest. Making this work almost certainly means sub-regions (the Marches, the Home Counties, the Danelaw, the Highlands), which is new data to author and balance.

THE BRAKE — Civ V's empire-wide happiness. In Civ V happiness is a single realm-wide pool, and taking more cities strains it, so expansion is self-limiting and a wide empire is a deliberate choice with a price. Here happiness is strictly per county, so a realm of twenty counties is no harder to hold than a realm of three.
⚠️ COUNTER: the manual is explicit that happiness is a per-county rating with per-county causes, and a realm-wide layer on top risks making local management feel irrelevant — the opposite of what a county-management game wants. A gentler version: distance from your capital, or a count of counties beyond some threshold, feeding the EXISTING per-county happiness rather than replacing it.

COST. The carrot is the cheapest idea in this whole set if three regions are enough, and a medium data job if they are not. The brake is medium and touches a system the manual pins down.
properties.name: OPEN — should holding territory have a shape: bonuses for coherent realms, strain for sprawling ones? (Risk + Civ V)
properties.rationale: Captured 2026-08-26. Recorded as one question rather than two because a carrot without a brake just makes snowballing faster, and a brake without a carrot just makes conquest annoying — they are the same design lever seen from both ends.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-27, from a military background: "the strongest military in the world is limited by logistics."

WHAT THE GAME ALREADY HAS, so this is a correction rather than a new system. Armies forage the county they stand in and starve when it cannot feed them. Supply convoys carry grain from a friendly county to an army, travel the map tile by tile, can be intercepted by an enemy standing on their path, and unload into the army's carried supply. The bones of logistics are built.

WHAT IS MISSING, AND IT IS THE CENTRAL FACT OF PRE-MODERN LOGISTICS. A convoy delivers the same load whether it travelled one county or the length of Britain. It costs nothing to move. In reality the cart and its animals eat the cargo: the classic figure, from Engels on Alexander and van Creveld's Supplying War, is that a pack animal carries roughly 250 lb and eats about 10 lb a day, so a column exhausts its own load in something like twenty-five days out and back. THERE IS A RADIUS BEYOND WHICH LAND SUPPLY IS ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE, and every medieval campaign was shaped by it.

THE IDEA. A convoy consumes food per tile travelled, by its own escort and draught animals. Short hauls arrive nearly full; long ones arrive nearly empty; past some distance the wagon eats everything and there is no point setting out. Supply range becomes a real, computable limit rather than a flavour note.

⚠️ THE COUNTER-INTUITIVE PART, AND WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. This makes deep offensives HARDER, and the harness has just measured that offensives already stall — so on its face it makes the game's worst problem worse. But the current stall is a UNIFORM grind: every part of the front is equally impossible. A supply radius does not make campaigning impossible, it makes it POSSIBLE IN SOME PLACES AND NOT OTHERS. That converts a featureless meat grinder into geography, which is what a war game wants. It should be judged on that, and it is a real risk if the radius is set too tight.

COST. Small in code — a per-tile deduction inside a convoy step that already walks the route. Large in consequence, and it wants the harness run before and after.
properties.name: OPEN — the tyranny of the wagon: a convoy should eat its own load

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-27 alongside the wagon question, and the two only really work together. SHARPENED the same day with the Viking evidence, which is the strongest case in British history for what water does to a campaign.

THE HISTORICAL FACT, and it is enormous. Water carriage was cheaper than land by something between one and two orders of magnitude — Diocletian's Price Edict implies sea freight at a small fraction of cart freight over the same distance, and river carriage sat between. Every large medieval operation that succeeded was on water. Edward III held the siege of CALAIS for eleven months in 1346-47 because he could supply it by sea; no army could have been fed there overland for a fortnight. Edward I's conquest of Wales was built on sea-supplied castles — Harlech, Beaumaris and Caernarfon all sited so a ship could reach them. When King John lost Normandy he lost the river network that fed it.

⚠️ AND THE VIKINGS ARE THE PROOF THAT IT IS NOT JUST A COASTAL EFFECT. The longship's genius was its SHALLOW DRAUGHT: it needed no harbour and drew little enough water to be rowed far up rivers that no other fleet could enter. That is how they reached York up the Ouse, Nottingham up the Trent, and Paris up the Seine. It meant England had no safe interior — a country that thought itself protected by distance from the sea discovered its rivers were roads pointing inward. So this idea is not "coastal counties are privileged". It is that the RIVER NETWORK IS A MAP OF WHERE ARMIES CAN REACH AND BE FED, and the interior uplands with no navigable water are the parts that are genuinely hard to campaign in. That is a far more interesting map than a rim.

WHY IT FITS THIS GAME PARTICULARLY. Britain is an island with a real coastline now, and the map already carries rivers on hex edges and Coast as a terrain type. The geography is sitting there unused by the supply system: convoys path over land like everyone else and a river is merely an obstacle costing extra to cross. Turning water from a barrier into a road is largely a matter of reading a map that already exists.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It is the larger of the two ideas: convoys use ordinary land pathfinding, so this wants a second cost model and a notion of which water is navigable — the map has Coast and river edges but no navigability, and following a river drawn on hex EDGES rather than tiles is fiddly to route along.
The Viking sharpening cuts against the "coastal realms are favoured" worry but replaces it with a harder question: which rivers are navigable how far inland? Get that wrong and either everywhere is reachable or nowhere is.
And it would interact with ferries, which already move armies across declared sea links; two water systems that do not know about each other would be a mess.

COST. Medium to large, and clearly the biggest of the logistics ideas. Worth doing after the wagon, because the wagon alone tells you whether a supply radius works at all.
properties.name: OPEN — water is the artery: sea and river supply, and why campaigns follow the coast

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Distinct from dec:idea-player-authored-objects: that asks whether the player should be able to author objects at all; this asks where the model executes if they can. This one has to be answered even for the smallest version of the feature, and it collides with two things the design already holds.

THE TWO COLLISIONS, stated plainly:
- req:offline-mobile-play and con:offline-no-network say the Android build plays fully offline with no network. A model call is a network call.
- req:deterministic-sim says the simulation is deterministic from a seed. An LLM is not deterministic.

Options:
(a) AUTHORING-TIME ONLY, ONLINE, RESULT CACHED AS DATA. The player writes the concept while connected; the model returns a validated struct; the struct is saved into the scenario/save file and from then on it is ordinary game data. The deterministic core never sees a model and never calls out. This resolves BOTH collisions cleanly — determinism survives because the sim only ever consumes the frozen blob, and offline play survives because authoring is a separate act from playing. Cheapest, and the only option that leaves the existing requirements intact.
(b) ON-DEVICE SMALL MODEL. Preserves offline authoring, but fights the APK size and the phone's memory and battery hard, and a small model is much worse at emitting a valid constrained struct. Much larger, and it buys only the ability to author while offline.
(c) MODEL IN THE TURN LOOP — the LLM consulted while the game runs. Breaks determinism outright and makes offline play impossible. Recorded for completeness, not because it looks viable.

A NOTE THAT MAKES (a) MORE ATTRACTIVE THAN IT FIRST LOOKS: authoring-time-only also means the authored object is inspectable and editable as plain data. The player can see exactly what the model decided, and change it. That is probably better design than a black box, independent of the offline argument.

THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO ALL OF THEM: this puts a dependency on someone else's API into a project that has deliberately been built dependency-free and offline. Even confined to authoring time, it is the first thing in the game that stops working if a key expires or a service changes.
properties.name: OPEN — if an LLM populates game objects, where does it run and when

SETTLED by Ajs on 2026-08-26: "Britain only."

The game ships one land, Great Britain, and does not carry the original's other maps (Scotland, Ireland, France, the Holy Roman Empire). Effort goes into making the one map good rather than into a map pipeline that carries five.

WHAT IT COSTS, RECORDED HONESTLY. The original treated each map as a BALANCE problem — Ireland balanced for four players with every start touching two neutral counties, Scotland deliberately nasty with only ten counties, France hardest from the Royal Demesne. One map means one balance, and the current Britain map has no stated balance intent at all: it is real historic counties with hand-placed grid positions. If replayability later feels thin, this decision is where to look first, and the answer then is more likely "state Britain's balance intent" than "add France".

NOT IRREVERSIBLE. Nothing here forbids a second map later; it says one is not being built now, and that the map machinery should not be generalised in advance for maps that do not exist.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Ajs's idea, 2026-08-27 — how the Vikings moved so fast across England.

THE HISTORICAL FACT, and it is the hinge of the whole Viking period. For seventy years Norse raiders came in summer and went home in autumn, and England survived them. Then in 865 the Great Heathen Army landed in East Anglia, SEIZED HORSES on arrival, and — the thing that changed everything — DID NOT GO HOME. It wintered in fortified camps on English soil: Torksey in 872-73, Repton in 873-74, both since dug and confirmed as large defended enclosures beside navigable water. An army that overwinters where it stands begins the next campaigning season already in position, with no crossing to make and no ground to retake. Within a decade three of the four English kingdoms were gone. The mechanism was not better fighting. It was not going home.

THE IDEA. Let an army fortify where it stands in enemy territory — dig in, become a supply point, survive the winter, and start next season from there instead of falling back. A forward base rather than a raid that must return.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THE MEASURED PROBLEM, and this is why I would rank it high. The harness found offensives that stall because an army deep in enemy land cannot be reinforced — the AI tops up only armies on friendly soil, so every push runs out of steam and falls back to where it started. A fortified camp IS the answer the period found to exactly that: it converts a raid into a foothold, gives supply somewhere to arrive, and makes the next season's fighting start from the ground you took rather than the ground you left.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
It cuts against the campaign-season idea recorded beside it: one says armies should be forced out of the field in winter, the other says the interesting move is refusing to leave. They can both be true — wintering in the field should be POSSIBLE and EXPENSIVE, which is what it actually was — but that has to be designed deliberately rather than discovered as a contradiction.
It also risks making conquest too easy by removing the natural rhythm of advance and consolidation, and it partly duplicates what castles already do. The difference worth keeping is that a camp is fast, temporary and built by the army, where a castle is slow, permanent and built by a county.

COST. Small to medium. Sieges already keep an army in place for seasons and foraging already feeds it from the land, so the parts exist; what is new is the fortifying, the supply-point status, and what winter does to a camp.
properties.name: OPEN — the Viking winter camp: what turns raiding into conquest

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Raised 2026-08-26 on Ajs's instruction to keep the economics medieval.

WOOL WAS THE ENGLISH ECONOMY. Not grain — grain fed people, wool paid for everything else. English fleeces were the best in Europe, and the trade to the Flemish weaving towns was so central that the export duty on it funded the crown's wars, that the Lord Chancellor still sits on a Woolsack, and that Edward III could bankrupt Florentine banks by defaulting on loans secured against it. Monasteries ran flocks in the thousands. A county with sheep on its uplands was rich in a way a county with wheat was not.

WHAT THE GAME HAS. Cattle on pasture, for beef and dairy, and nothing else from an animal. The map already carries a Pasture tile resource and the moors and hills that real English sheep grazed — the Pennines, the Welsh uplands, the Downs. Wool would be the first good the realm produces to SELL rather than to eat, which is a different economic verb from anything currently in the game, and it gives the marketplace something the buy side actually wants.

CREDIT, AND THE PROBLEM WITH IT. The Church forbade usury — lending at interest was a sin, and for most of the period an offence. But rulers needed money in a hurry, so credit existed in the shapes the ban allowed: Jewish moneylenders under royal protection until Edward I expelled them in 1290 and voided what was owed them, then Italian bankers, the Riccardi and the Frescobaldi and the Bardi, lending against future wool duties and being ruined in their turn when kings defaulted. Loans were dressed as sales, as leases, as penalties for late repayment — anything but interest.

THE IDEA. A ruler in trouble can borrow — quickly, at a punishing effective rate, from a lender whose protection is itself a political act. Repay and your credit stands. Default, or expel the lender and cancel the debt, and you have gold today, no credit tomorrow, and a reputation the other nobles can see. That last move is not a designer's cynicism; it is what actually happened, twice.

⚠️ COUNTERS.
Wool is the safer and better of the two: it is a new good, a new use for pasture, and a reason for the market's buy side to exist, all without touching a working system. But it is new CONTENT — a production chain, a price, tiles, UI — not a tuning change.
Credit is the more dangerous. A loan is a way to escape a losing position, and a game where you can always borrow out of trouble is a game with less tension, not more. It only works if default genuinely costs something the player values — which, with diplomacy already modelling reputation, is at least possible here.
Neither is in the manual, and the expulsion mechanic in particular touches real history that a game should handle with some care rather than as a clever exploit.

COST. Wool: medium, and mostly content. Credit: small in code, large in balance, and it needs the reputation consequence to land or it is simply free money.
properties.name: OPEN — wool and the moneylenders: England's real economy, and credit without usury

properties.alternatives: Bundling a Node server into the APK; requiring a network connection.
properties.decision: A second implementation of the backend interface dispatches commands directly against an in-memory state inside the browser or WebView, exposing exactly the shape the HTTP client does.

properties.rationale: It is what lets the game run fully offline — packaged as a mobile APK with no network — since the core is pure, deterministic TypeScript. The REST routes and store remain 'the port of record for this logic'.

properties.decision: types hold data only, systems hold logic only, state builds data; each system is independently testable and imports only what it needs; clients import the barrel and never a system file.
properties.name: One seasonal concern per file, data and logic separated
properties.rationale: Recorded as following from a project preference for non-monolithic code, and it is what lets a feature be added as one system file plus one test file.

properties.decision: Parsers for the original game's files are committed; their output is gitignored and must not be published. Functional facts are reusable, the original pixel art is not.
properties.name: Decode the original data to learn from it, never to ship it
properties.rationale: An intellectual-property boundary: the tools exist to understand and analyse the original data so original content can be authored, not to redistribute the original assets.

properties.alternatives: Deleting the legacy scenes outright; keeping Phaser as the primary renderer.
properties.decision: The DOM/SVG UI is the game; the original Phaser scene shell boots only with ?phaser=1, is dynamically imported, and its failures are caught so they cannot take the UI down.
properties.name: Demote the Phaser canvas to an opt-in flag
properties.rationale: Keeps roughly a megabyte of Phaser out of the default bundle and stops WebGL initialisation ever running — or erroring — in the normal game.

properties.decision: The legacy Phaser scenes and their extracted art stay in the repository as reference material to look at. They are not going back into the game and are not a capability the system provides.
properties.name: Keep the Phaser shell as reference material, not as a capability
properties.rationale: Stated by the project owner. The scenes only boot behind ?phaser=1, nothing in the game loop reaches them, and no requirement asks for them — but they are worth keeping to look at rather than deleting.

properties.decision: The Express REST service, its in-memory store, its Zod wire schemas and the generated OpenAPI document are retired, together with the renderer's HTTP client. The in-process backend is the one backend the game has.
properties.name: Retire the REST service; the in-process backend is the product
properties.rationale: The server was genuinely built, works, and passes 17 of its own tests — but nothing consumes it. The shipping client imports the in-process backend at module level, so there is no runtime path to the HTTP client at all, and the browser end-to-end suite passes in full with the API server stopped. Offline-first play overtook the frontend/backend split that the server was built to serve. Retired on the record rather than deleted, because it was real and the hosted-multiplayer goal it belonged to may return.

properties.decision: All randomness comes from a seeded RNG whose state can be captured and restored; even game ids are generated from a counter rather than a clock.
properties.name: No Math.random or Date.now in the core path
properties.rationale: Determinism is what makes save/load resume exactly, tests reproducible, and lockstep multiplayer possible.

properties.decision: The game is decided when one realm is left standing, when the human is eliminated, or when nobody survives. Dominating the map is explicitly not a win while any rival lives.
properties.name: Victory only by total conquest
properties.rationale: Recorded in the commit that introduced it and guarded by a test that asserts map domination does not win.

properties.decision: Each command handler validates and applies as one step, returning {ok:false,error} and leaving state untouched on rejection, instead of a separate validation pass.
properties.name: Validate and apply inside the same handler
properties.rationale: An invalid command can then never half-apply, and the discriminated union keeps routing exhaustive and type-checked.

properties.decision: Vite serves and builds the renderer and, through a plugin, the Electron main process; the renderer builds with relative asset paths.
properties.name: Move the build to Vite
properties.rationale: Replaces the unmaintained electron-webpack, and the relative base is what lets the same bundle load from file:// for Electron and from a Capacitor WebView.

properties.alternatives: A hand-written OpenAPI document, or spec-first generation of the types.
properties.decision: One set of Zod schemas drives both runtime validation and the generated OpenAPI document, and each carries a compile-time assertion that it is structurally identical to the corresponding core type.
properties.name: Zod schemas are the single source of truth, guarded at compile time
properties.rationale: So the spec can never silently misrepresent the API: if the core Command, GameState or TurnReport changes without the schema, or the reverse, the type-check fails.

The balance harness IS this project's validation instrument, and ver:balance-baseline was reclassified kind=validation on 2026-08-28 to say so. properties.statement: A ruler can trade with a merchant when one is present in a county they own, buying what the realm lacks and selling what it has spare — grain, cattle, wood, stone, iron and every kind of weapon. Merchants travel between counties on set circuits, so a well-placed county sees one often and a remote one rarely, and the price to buy is meaningfully higher than the price to sell. This gives the treasury both a purpose and a source: gold becomes something to spend, and a surplus becomes something other than a number that grows.

properties.source: Ajs, 2026-08-27: "the strongest military in the world is limited by logistics (ability to supply your troops in the front lines)" — promoted with "let's go with your read; the wagon first"

Past some range the column consumes everything it carries and there is no point setting out at all. Supply therefore has a finite, computable radius from wherever it was raised, and where a realm can sustain a campaign becomes a question about geography rather than a question about willpower.

properties.description:
Twenty AI-versus-AI games, three nobles, default aggression, played to a FIVE-HUNDRED-turn cap — a hundred and twenty-five game years each. Kept as the line every later balance change is measured against.

THE CAP WAS 200 TURNS (fifty years) until 2026-08-28. It was raised because making all four rulers genuinely competitive made games harder to resolve rather than easier — a contested map takes longer to settle than a walkover — and on the same twenty seeds only 1/20 games reached a decision inside 200 turns against 5/20 inside 500, resolving between turns 151 and 409. A cap most games cannot reach measures the cap rather than the design.

⚠️ FIGURES RECORDED BEFORE THAT DATE ARE NOT COMPARABLE WITH FIGURES AFTER IT. Everything in this design's history up to 2026-08-28 was measured at 200 turns; `npm run balance -- --turns 200` reproduces the old standard. The run also takes roughly two and a half times as long.
properties.findings:
FIRST RUN AT THE NEW 500-TURN CAP, 2026-08-28. Still failing, but this is the first honest measurement of decisiveness — the old 200-turn cap was cutting games off before the design had resolved them.

  reached a decision   5/20 (25%), resolving at turns 151-409, median 241
  undecided            15, leader holding 59% of the map at the cap
  sieges laid          177 (61-330), won 168

AND THE FIRST COMEBACK EVER MEASURED. "Winner took the lead" now reads 0 (0-9) where every previous run in this design's history read 0 (0-0) — in at least one game the eventual winner was not ahead from the first turn. One game out of twenty is not a comeback mechanic working, but it is the first time the number has not been unanimous.

A SEAT BIAS WORTH WATCHING: seat p1 won 4 of the 5 decided games. Five games is far too small to conclude anything, but if it holds at a larger sample it means the starting position decides the game, which would matter more than any of the balance work above.

WHAT THE LONGER RUN MAKES VISIBLE, and neither is new — both simply scale with the turns played: hungry county-seasons 15,145 and plagues 1,206 across 125 years. Per-year those are in line with the 200-turn figures.

UNCHANGED: upkeep never bites (0% of purse, 0 short paydays); MAX_ARMY_TARGET still caps a 40-county realm at 250 men per army; the population absorbing state is still open; the coalition mechanic's effect on outcomes is still unproven.

properties.description: A scripted pass through every facet a player can reach in the browser: the four county controls and the bulk realm controls, forging, mustering, hiring mercenaries, selecting and ordering armies, supply convoys, all four diplomacy actions, the marketplace across several goods, saving, the turn log, custom game setup with five nobles and hard difficulty and both advanced options, fog of war, castle building, and long unattended runs of fifteen and sixty turns. Records what works, what does not, and what is simply missing.
properties.findings:
Run 2026-08-26, overnight. No console errors anywhere across every facet.

WORKS: all four county controls (tax, ration, industry share, diet) and the bulk realm versions; forging, mustering and hiring mercenaries; selecting armies and ordering marches; supply convoys; all four diplomacy actions against every rival; the marketplace with prices quoted per good and per place; saving; the turn log; custom setup at five nobles, hard difficulty, weak counties, advanced farming and fog together; fog blacking out 6,697 of 6,840 tiles and leaving exactly the player's own counties visible; sixty unattended turns without a stumble.

THREE THINGS THE SWEEP FOUND.

1. THE STACKED-ARMY BUG HAD COME BACK, at three armies rather than two. The fan-out that fixed it used a flat radius of 3.4 map units against a banner 7 units wide: enough to separate two, not three, so mustering twice in one county made the banners unclickable again. The radius is now DERIVED from the geometry — n banners on a ring sit 2*r*sin(pi/n) apart, so the radius that separates them is the icon width over that — and past six the banners shrink instead of spilling into the next hex. The regression test now musters three, not two, which is the number that would have caught it.

2. CASTLE BUILDING WAS UNREACHABLE. BuildCastle has existed in the command protocol since it was written, is covered by the simulation tests, and the manual lists building castles as one of the six things a ruler does each turn — but no control ever invoked it, so a county could only keep the castle it started with. This also quietly explains part of the economy finding: castles are the main sink for timber and stone, and the sink had no tap. A build control now offers all five designs with their costs and shows progress; verified building a Norman keep from order to standing, with the realm's stone visibly drawn to nothing and recovering.

3. WOOL WAS INVISIBLE. Newly added and pooling correctly — 648 fleeces by turn 12 — but the treasury readout still listed only gold, timber, stone and iron, so the player had no way to know it existed.

TWO FINDINGS LEFT OPEN, both balance rather than defect. A passive player survives sixty turns against three rivals at maximum AI aggression, so the AI cannot close out a game against someone doing nothing. And materials still accumulate without limit even with a castle built — 2,475 timber and 504 stone by turn 20 — because one castle per county is a finite sink against unbounded production.

properties.description: Six game years played through the browser UI twice — once trading actively, once touching nothing — with the realm's books read off the HUD every four turns, plus a headless run of the same 24 turns to read the county stores the HUD does not show. Asks not whether the market works but whether it is worth using.
properties.findings:
RE-RUN 2026-08-26 after supply-and-demand pricing and the merchant's purse. The exploit is closed and trade has become a decision.

THE SAME GOOD NOW HAS DIFFERENT PRICES IN DIFFERENT PLACES. After 24 turns: Berkshire holds 6,629 sacks against a usual 516 and grain sells there for 1 crown; Wiltshire holds 25,060 against 9,860 and gets 2; Hampshire holds 3,022 against a usual 11,468 and pays 7. A sack is worth seven times more one county away, so where and when to sell is now the question rather than whether.

THE GLUT IS PRICED IN. Timber held 3,066 against a usual 240 sits at the 0.2 floor — buy 2, sell 1. Hoarding is visibly worthless, which is the honest answer to a production line that never stops.

THE MONEY PRINTER IS CAPPED. Selling everything a wagon would take, every visit, for six years: 940 sacks for 2,744 crowns across 12 visits. Against the earlier finding that one county's granary was worth 76,365, that is the exploit gone. Trade played hard roughly triples tax income — strong, bounded, and it takes deliberate effort.

ONE CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING, and it is the model working rather than a fault: a realm holding none of a material is a desperate buyer and pays up to three times for it. At turn 0 with no timber, wood costs 24 a unit against 200 starting gold. Two turns of your own production fixes it, so early scarcity is a texture rather than a wall — but it does mean you cannot shop your way out of the opening.
